title: Workflow-friendly free-breathing whole-chest cardiovascular MRI using inner-volume balanced T1 relaxation-enhanced steady-state.
abstract: Background Free-breathing cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) may provide useful volumetric information. This study evaluated acquisition time and the feasibility of incorporating highly accelerated free-breathing inner-volume balanced T1 relaxation-enhanced steady-state (bT1RESS) imaging into a standard CMR protocol during the post-contrast interval before late gadolinium enhancement (LGE). Methods A prototype ECG-gated, navigator-gated inner-volume bT1RESS sequence was added to 1.5T CMR examinations in 45 patients; 30 were included in the paired comparison with breath-hold bT1RESS. Series-start timing was assessed in 14 of the 45 patients. Three readers assessed image quality. Aortic diameters were compared between bT1RESS protocols and, in an additional cohort of 15 subjects, with CEMRA. Agreement was assessed separately at five aortic levels using Bland-Altman analysis. Results Median inner-volume bT1RESS acquisition time was 1.82minutes (range, 0.78-3.72). In the series-start timing subset, median intervals from perfusion/CEMRA start to TI scout and first LGE series were 6.49minutes (n=13) and 8.46minutes (n=14), respectively. Reader preferences favored the inner-volume over breath-hold bT1RESS protocol. In the CEMRA comparison, mean differences (inner-volume bT1RESS minus CEMRA) ranged from 0.00 to 0.93mm; the lower and upper 95% limits of agreement ranged from -2.47 to -1.16mm and from 2.06 to 3.02mm, respectively. Conclusion Inner-volume bT1RESS provided rapid volumetric cardiovascular imaging within the evaluated post-contrast workflow. A primary benefit is the capability for 3D vessel measurement without a separate first-pass CEMRA acquisition. The technique may also help identify coronary artery origins, characterize morphological abnormalities in congenital heart disease and other cardiovascular disorders, and help to detect and characterize extracardiac lesions. Larger studies are needed to establish reproducibility and diagnostic performance.

title: Dynamic Fractional Myocardial Blood Volume Mapping Using Ferumoxytol-enhanced CMR Multitasking with Subspace Dose Harmonization.
abstract: Background Fractional myocardial blood volume (fMBV) represents the vascular compartment within myocardial tissue and may reflect changes in microvascular status and health. Conventionally derived from multi-dose Modified Look-Locker Inversion (MOLLI) recovery T1 mapping with ferumoxytol, MOLLI-based fMBV requires repeated breath-holds, inter-dose image registration, and static end-diastolic estimates. CMR Multitasking enables free-breathing, non-electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated imaging and offers a subspace that captures shared motion and contrast dynamics. This subspace representation can be exploited to harmonize multi-dose acquisitions directly in parameter space, enabling motion-resolved dynamic fMBV mapping while reducing reliance on post-hoc image-space registration. Methods Thirteen healthy volunteers (11 females, 28.2±10.0 years) and twelve ischemic heart disease (IHD) patients (1 female, 67.2±7.1 years) underwent multi-dose ferumoxytol imaging at 3.0T using both breath-held ECG-triggered 5(3)3(3)3 MOLLI and free-running 2-dimensional Multitasking T1 mapping sequences. MOLLI-Multitasking agreement was assessed in healthy volunteers; patient data were used for exploratory dynamic fMBV analysis. Multitasking data were harmonized across respiratory- and cardiac-motion subspace dimensions for cross-dose alignment. Pixel-wise fMBV was estimated using a two-compartment water exchange model. fMBV agreement with MOLLI was assessed using Bland-Altman analysis. Dynamic fMBV changes were also evaluated from the Multitasking data. In IHD patients, fMBV kinetic metrics (upslope and diastolic-to-systolic distribution) for cycle-dependent variation in dynamic fMBV were computed to assess systolic compression and diastolic recoil. Cardiac positron emission tomography (PET) derived perfusion and CMR-derived strain and late gadolinium enhancement served as references. Results In healthy volunteers, Multitasking produced motion-resolved fMBV maps with strong MOLLI agreement (bias -0.11%, p=0.84). Subspace harmonization reduced cross-dose variability and aligned cardiac phases. Healthy subjects showed significant diastolic-to-systolic variation (10.55±2.12% vs. 7.73±2.76%, p=0.0004). In IHD patients, ischemic segments exhibited elevated diastolic fMBV with significant systolic compression (16.36±3.44% vs. 10.01±2.24%, p=0.013), remote myocardium showed similar phasic variation (11.16±0.68% vs. 7.98±0.57%, p<0.0001). At the same time, scar demonstrated reduced fMBV with attenuated modulation (7.74±1.95% vs. 5.59±1.97%, p=0.099). Abnormal dynamic fMBV regions corresponded to PET defects and impaired circumferential strain. Conclusion Ferumoxytol-enhanced Multitasking with subspace harmonization enables free-breathing, cardiac-resolved dynamic fMBV mapping, overcoming practical limitations of MOLLI-derived fMBV. This approach enables non-invasive assessment of dynamic myocardial blood volume across the cardiac cycle, with potential utility for characterizing microvascular function in ischemic heart disease.

title: Precision localization of spinal cord lesions during surgery: Current technologies and future directions for targeted therapies.
abstract: Background Accurate intraoperative localization is essential for safe spinal cord surgery. Although numerous imaging, navigation, and neurophysiological technologies are available, their contributions are generally discussed individually rather than according to the information they provide for surgical decision-making. Emerging targeted intramedullary therapies introduce additional requirements for precise therapeutic delivery. Objective To critically review established and emerging intraoperative guidance technologies in spinal cord surgery and propose an information-centered framework supporting indication-specific surgical decision-making and precision therapeutic targeting. Methods A narrative review of the literature was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, supplemented by relevant references from selected publications. Technologies were evaluated according to their clinical applications, supporting evidence, limitations, and contribution to intraoperative guidance. Results Five complementary information domains were identified: anatomical localization, morphological characterization, functional localization, tissue characterization, and precision therapeutic targeting. Established techniques, particularly intraoperative ultrasound and neurophysiological monitoring, provide clinically relevant guidance in selected spinal cord procedures. Fluorescence imaging offers additional vascular or tumor-associated information, whereas advanced optical imaging, multimodal fusion, artificial intelligence, and robotic assistance remain insufficiently validated for routine intramedullary applications. The proposed framework emphasizes that these domains are neither mandatory nor sequential and that additional technological complexity does not necessarily translate into improved clinical outcomes. Emerging targeted therapies further highlight the distinction between instrument positioning accuracy, therapeutic deposition, and effective biological exposure. Conclusions An information-centered approach may help guide the selection and integration of intraoperative technologies according to surgical objectives and clinical evidence. Future developments should prioritize validated, indication-specific strategies demonstrating improvements in procedural safety, targeting accuracy, and patient-relevant outcomes.

Five complementary information domains were identified: anatomical localization, morphological characterization, functional localization, tissue characterization, and precision therapeutic targeting. Established techniques, particularly intraoperative ultrasound and neurophysiological monitoring, provide clinically relevant guidance in selected spinal cord procedures. Fluorescence imaging offers additional vascular or tumor-associated information, whereas advanced optical imaging, multimodal fusion, artificial intelligence, and robotic assistance remain insufficiently validated for routine intramedullary applications. The proposed framework emphasizes that these domains are neither mandatory nor sequential and that additional technological complexity does not necessarily translate into improved clinical outcomes. Emerging targeted therapies further highlight the distinction between instrument positioning accuracy, therapeutic deposition, and effective biological exposure.

Conclusions

An information-centered approach may help guide the selection and integration of intraoperative technologies according to surgical objectives and clinical evidence. Future developments should prioritize validated, indication-specific strategies demonstrating improvements in procedural safety, targeting accuracy, and patient-relevant outcomes.

title: Percutaneous screw distraction versus open fusion surgery for anatomic restoration after burst fracture.
abstract: Background Open posterior transpedicular screw fixation for thoracolumbar burst fractures involves substantial muscle dissection, resulting in iatrogenic trauma, prolonged hospital stays, and extended recovery times, but minimally invasive techniques like percutaneous pedicle screw fixation cannot be used in all fracture patterns or indications. We compared perioperative and radiographic outcomes of a fixed-angle percutaneous instrumentation technique versus conventional open fixation in patients managed without direct decompression. Methods In this retrospective cohort study at our Level I trauma center, patients who underwent either open or percutaneous instrumentation without laminectomy in 2018-2024 were identified. Patients with AO Spine fracture classifications of A2, A3, and A4 were present in the cohort. Student's t-test and Pearson's Chi-square statistical tests were used to compare the perioperative and radiographic outcomes of patients who underwent fixed-angle percutaneous instrumentation with those who underwent conventional open fixation without direct decompression. Results Among 63 included patients, 24 underwent percutaneous surgery and 39 had open procedures. Selection varied by on-call surgeon, not fracture characteristics. AO Spine fracture classifications (A2, A3, A4) were similarly distributed between groups (p = 0.25). Baseline characteristics were similar between groups. The percutaneous group experienced significantly less intraoperative blood loss (p < 0.001), showed greater improvement in canal cross-sectional area from preoperative to postoperative (p = 0.01), and had greater improvement in vertebral body index scores from postdistraction to last follow-up (p = 0.02). The groups were statistically similar in all other radiographic outcomes. Elective instrumentation removal was more frequent in patients in the percutaneous cohort (p = 0.001). Conclusions Percutaneous instrumentation for thoracolumbar burst fractures not involving decompression achieved radiographic outcomes comparable with open techniques in this study. The percutaneous technique demonstrated favorable radiographic outcomes, with greater indirect canal decompression intraoperatively and better vertebral body index scores at last follow-up. These findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant prospective comparison.

title: Subtype-specific radiographic outcomes following posterior decompression for degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis based on the CARDS classification.
abstract: Purpose The management of degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis (DLS) remains controversial due to concerns regarding postoperative instability. This study aimed to evaluate whether the Clinical and Radiographic Degenerative Spondylolisthesis (CARDS) classification can predict changes in vertebral translation and intervertebral alignment following posterior decompression without fusion. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 82 patients who underwent posterior decompression across 162 spinal segments, comprising 125 segments with DLS (classified into CARDS Types A-D) and 37 non-spondylolisthesis (Non-DS) segments. Radiographic parameters, including vertebral translation, intervertebral lordosis, and disc height, were evaluated preoperatively and at one-year follow-up. Primary analyses compared radiographic changes among the 125 DLS segments according to CARDS subtypes using linear mixed-effects models. Results Overall, decompression did not lead to a significant increase in vertebral translation. However, subtype analysis among DLS segments revealed distinct patterns: CARDS Types A and C segments showed a significant reduction in vertebral translation and an increase in intervertebral lordosis. In contrast, Type D segments demonstrated significant progression of vertebral translation postoperatively, despite achieving gains in lordosis similar to other types. Type A segments also showed a significant increase in postoperative disc height. Conclusion The CARDS classification effectively identifies distinct radiographic responses to decompression surgery. While Types A and C tend to maintain or improve alignment, Type D is associated with a higher risk of progressive translation. These findings suggest that CARDS subtype-specific characteristics should be considered when assessing the risk of postoperative instability.

title: Callosal atrophy does not establish physiological disconnection in imaging models of cognitive risk in multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Automated magnetic resonance imaging can quantify callosal atrophy and estimate structural disconnection in multiple sclerosis, but neither measurement establishes physiological conduction failure. In an early relapsing-remitting cohort, Wahl and colleagues found a relationship between motor-callosal microstructure and interhemispheric inhibition in controls that was not detectable in patients. This finding illustrates why a structural feature cannot automatically inherit a functional interpretation. Earlier structure-function studies provide a foundation for contemporary pipelines when the measurements, pathways, and populations are comparable. This opinion paper organizes validation into five evidence domains with separate biological and prognostic branches: technical validity, biological validity, physiological validity, prognostic performance, and clinical utility. Physiological claims require functional evidence matched to anatomy and task, with reliability and competing circuit explanations assessed. A purely prognostic feature instead requires credible predictive evaluation, including external validation and calibration; it may be useful as a proxy for global disease burden. Clinical utility concerns the consequences of a specified decision and is distinct from predictive performance and implementation feasibility. Reports should preserve the qualifier in estimated structural disconnection and reserve physiological interpretations for measurements supported by corresponding functional evidence.

title: Research on multimodal medical data fusion and application based on large-scale models.
abstract: The rapid advancement of large-scale artificial intelligence foundation models has demonstrated strong potential across a wide range of domains. In healthcare, disease diagnosis and prognostic assessment require the comprehensive integration of heterogeneous information from multiple sources, including laboratory tests, medical imaging, electronic health records, genomic profiles, as well as data from the four-diagnostic methods of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM). However, analyses based on a single modality are often insufficient to capture the complex biological mechanisms and clinical phenotypes underlying disease. To address this limitation, this review summarizes recent progress in multimodal medical data fusion enabled by large-scale models and highlights associated clinical applications in both Chinese and Western medicine. First, we clearly define the current state of medical large-scale models, outline major medical data modalities, review key technologies, and elaborate four classic multimodal fusion strategies. Second, we survey advances in core clinical scenarios of Chinese and Western medicine, and correlate each research case with corresponding fusion taxonomies, with in-depth discussion of model design and existing limitations. Third, we expound the digital acquisition and representation of data from the four diagnostic methods of TCM, multimodal fusion modeling for syndrome differentiation, preventive treatment and personalized medication, and further compare the differences between Chinese and Western medicine in diagnostic logic, modality heterogeneity, and fusion requirements. Finally, we analyze unique challenges specific to multimodal fusion in large-scale models including medical data quality, privacy and ethical risks, cross-modal alignment and poor interpretability, and outline targeted future directions. This review aims to provide a systematic reference for clinicians and researchers engaged in integrating Chinese and Western medicine and promote the responsible deployment of large-scale models in clinical practice. Please cite this article as: Zhao N, Li YQ, Liu H. Research on multimodal medical data fusion and application based on large-scale models. J Integr Med. 2026; Epub ahead of print.

title: External Fixation of a Pediatric Mandibular Fracture Using a Patient-Specific 3-Dimensional-Printed Splint Based on Virtual Surgical Planning.
abstract: Mandibular fractures in young children are challenging because of ongoing craniofacial growth, developing dentition, and the limitations of internal fixation. We report the use of a patient-specific splint based on virtual surgical planning in a 5-year-old boy with fractures of the right parasymphysis and left mental-foramen region. Computed tomography data were used for 3-dimensional reconstruction, virtual fracture reduction, and splint design, followed by 3-dimensional printing with medical-grade photosensitive resin. Postoperative evaluation showed satisfactory restoration of occlusion and fracture alignment, and healing was uneventful. This technique may provide an accurate and minimally invasive option for selected pediatric mandibular fractures when preservation of mandibular growth potential is a priority.

title: Hydraulic pressure sinus lift versus piezoelectric lift via lateral approach: A randomized controlled clinical trial.
abstract: Introduction To assess the effectiveness of hydraulic pressure sinus lift via lateral wall approach versus piezoelectric surgery in patients with deficient posterior maxilla. Materials and methods This study involved a randomized clinical trial of 20 participants with less than 6 mm of bone height in the posterior maxilla in need of Maxillary Sinus Floor Augmentation using the lateral window approach. Patients were randomly assigned to two groups; the HPLT Group included 10 patients who underwent hydraulic pressure for osteotomy preparation for the lateral sinus lifting technique, while the PSLT Group included 10 patients managed using piezoelectric surgery. Clinical and radiographic assessment of bone augmentation, as well as intraoperative biological complications and postoperative complications, were recorded. Results Both groups showed insignificant differences in the recorded procedural duration, intraoperative complications, and reported postoperative pain. The HPLT group reported a statistically significant increase in bone height, with a mean height gain of 6.81 ± 1.85. The PSLT group reported a mean height gain of 5.51 ± 0.90. The difference between the compared groups regarding the final gain in bone height was statistically insignificant (P = 0.061). Discussion Both hydraulic pressure-assisted and piezoelectric lateral sinus floor elevation resulted in increased radiographic bone height at six months, without a statistically significant difference between groups. Although these findings support the feasibility of hydraulic pressure-assisted sinus augmentation, the limited sample size prevents definitive conclusions regarding its comparative effectiveness and safety.

title: Modified Osteotomy Strategies for Severe Mandibular Retrognathism with OSAHS: A Proof-of-Concept Case Study.
abstract: Objectives The study aimed to explore the biomechanical effects of different mandibular distraction osteogenesis (MDO) on the temporomandibular joint (TMJ), and evaluate its improvement on upper airway ventilation in severe mandibular retrognathism patients with OSAHS, via biomechanical analysis of the TMJ based on multimodal data fusion and computational fluid dynamics (CFD). Methods One adult patient with skeletal Class II severe mandibular retrognathism and OSAHS was enrolled. CBCT and MRI data were collected to reconstruct the TMJ complex (including articular discs, masseter muscles) and upper airway. Two osteotomy designs (mandibular body DO vs. mandibular angle DO) were simulated to compare condylar stress patterns. Cephalometric and CBCT measurements were applied to assess skeletal, occlusal and TMJ morphological changes. Airway volumetric changes and aerodynamic parameters (velocity, pressure, resistance) at characteristic cross-sections were quantified via CFD. Results The mandibular body DO concentrated stress on the lateral condylar region, while the mandibular angle DO localized loading on the condylar apex and medioposterior slope. Postoperatively, adaptive condylar remodeling was observed with a 49.15% increase in lateral joint space. The ANB angle decreased by 54.7%, correcting severe skeletal Class II malocclusion to mild with improved facial profile. Total upper airway volume increased by 19.59%, mainly in the velopharynx and glossopharynx. CFD showed markedly reduced airflow velocity and airway resistance after treatment. Conclusion The mandibular body DO design appeared to achieve a biomechanically favorable condylar stress distribution in simulation, which may promote TMJ stability. Furthermore, moderate CFD-derived improvements in upper airway morphology and aerodynamics were observed; however, without postoperative polysomnography evaluation, these cannot be interpreted as objectively confirmed improvement in OSAHS severity, warranting validation in larger cohorts.

The mandibular body DO concentrated stress on the lateral condylar region, while the mandibular angle DO localized loading on the condylar apex and medioposterior slope. Postoperatively, adaptive condylar remodeling was observed with a 49.15% increase in lateral joint space. The ANB angle decreased by 54.7%, correcting severe skeletal Class II malocclusion to mild with improved facial profile. Total upper airway volume increased by 19.59%, mainly in the velopharynx and glossopharynx. CFD showed markedly reduced airflow velocity and airway resistance after treatment.

Conclusion

The mandibular body DO design appeared to achieve a biomechanically favorable condylar stress distribution in simulation, which may promote TMJ stability. Furthermore, moderate CFD-derived improvements in upper airway morphology and aerodynamics were observed; however, without postoperative polysomnography evaluation, these cannot be interpreted as objectively confirmed improvement in OSAHS severity, warranting validation in larger cohorts.

title: Ovary-Sparing Surgery for Coexisting Mature Cystic Teratoma and Ovarian Hemangioma in a 7-Year-Old Girl: A Case Report.
abstract: Study objective To describe ovary-sparing management of coexisting mature cystic teratoma and ovarian hemangioma in a child. Methods A 7-year-old girl with periumbilical pain and early pubertal signs underwent endocrine, radiologic, and surgical evaluation of a complex pelvic mass. Results Endocrine assessment, including age-concordant bone age, supported premature pubarche without evidence of central precocious puberty. An isolated inhibin B elevation normalized 12 days later before surgery and remained normal postoperatively; other tumor markers and hormones were normal. Serial imaging variably suggested uterine or ovarian origin. Left ovarian lesions were completely excised through a Pfannenstiel approach while preserving follicle-containing ovarian tissue. Final pathology demonstrated a 5.5-cm hemangioma adjacent to a 2.5-cm mature teratoma. Recovery was uneventful, with no recurrence or pubertal progression during 2 years of 6-monthly follow-up. Conclusion Decisions regarding ovary-sparing surgery should integrate preoperative clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings with intraoperative assessment; definitive histopathology establishes the final diagnosis.

title: Building plant 3D digital twins via AI-powered cell atlases: technological advances, applications, and future perspectives.
abstract: Plant organ function is governed by the precise spatial arrangement and coordinated interactions of constituent cells. Immobilized by rigid cell walls, plant cells develop in place, and their positions and adjacency relationships form a three-dimensional (3D) topological network that underpins tissue architecture and organ morphogenesis. Conventional two-dimensional (2D) sectioning, however, discretizes this continuous topology into isolated planes, severing native cell adjacency and obscuring global organ architecture, whereas volumetric imaging preserves cellular coordinates, geometry and connectivity in situ. Recent advances in multimodal cross-scale imaging have enabled high-resolution 3D visualization spanning from subcellular structures to intact organs. In parallel, deep-learning-based segmentation has increasingly resolved bottlenecks in densely packed plant tissues, facilitating the construction of computable digital cell atlases. In this review, we synthesize progress in the intelligent 3D interpretation of plant multicellular systems, surveying the technical capabilities of multimodal imaging regarding penetration depth, spatial resolution, and four-dimensional (4D) dynamic tracking, alongside deep-learning strategies to overcome structural constraints imposed by rigid cell walls. Furthermore, diverse applications of digital cell atlases in morphological phenotyping, mechanical inference, topological network analysis, and spatial multi-omics integration are examined, underscoring their role as the foundational data substrate for plant digital twins. We further distinguish digital cell atlases from predictive digital twins and highlight plant-specific challenges, including optical barriers of plant tissues, cross-lineage model transfer and deployment in breeding. We conclude by discussing the transition from static reconstructions toward predictive digital twins of plant tissues and organs, providing a methodological framework to elucidate plant organ morphogenesis.

title: Subfield-specific hippocampal enlargement in high-functioning autism spectrum disorder.
abstract: Background Although previous studies have reported abnormal hippocampal volumes in children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), the specific alterations in hippocampal subfields and their relationships with clinical symptoms in high-functioning ASD (HF-ASD) remain unclear. Methods In this study, we analyzed T1-weighted structural MRI data from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange I (ABIDE-I), including 182 children and adolescents with HF-ASD and 213 age- and sex-matched typically developing controls (TDC). Using a linear mixed-effects model, we compared hippocampal volumes between groups, and examined associations between volumes and clinical measurements. Results Compared to TDC, the children and adolescents with HF-ASD exhibited significantly increased volumes in the right entire hippocampus, presubiculum, subiculum, and granule cell layer of the dentate gyrus (GC-DG). No significant volumetric differences were observed within the child or adolescent subgroups, nor between these age groups. Notably, presubiculum volume showed a positive correlation with verbal scores and a negative correlation with social scores in the HF-ASD group. Conclusions These findings indicate subfield-specific hippocampal overgrowth in children and adolescents with HF-ASD and presubiculum volume alteration may be a potential neuroanatomical correlate underlying verbal and social dysfunctions.

title: Proceedings from the 2025 International Consensus Meeting on Orthopedic Infections: Diagnosis of Periprosthetic Shoulder Infection.
abstract: Background Prosthetic joint infection (PJI) following shoulder arthroplasty is difficult to diagnose because clinical findings are often nonspecific, conventional diagnostic tests have variable sensitivity, and Cutibacterium acnes (C. acnes) may cause indolent infection with limited systemic inflammatory response. Diagnostic criteria have also largely been adapted from hip and knee arthroplasty with limited shoulder-specific validation. This International Consensus Meeting (ICM) reviewed the available evidence and developed consensus recommendations for the diagnosis of shoulder PJI. Methods The Shoulder Group of the 2025 ICM on Orthopedic Infections included international shoulder surgeons, infectious disease physicians, and microbiology experts experienced in shoulder arthroplasty and PJI. Thirty-two diagnostic questions underwent question-specific literature review, presentation to the consensus group, discussion, and voting. A modified Delphi process was used to establish consensus. Delegates voted to agree, disagree, or abstain. Consensus was categorized by percentage agreement, while strength of recommendation was assessed separately based on evidence quality, consistency, and directness. Results Consensus was achieved for 31 analyzed questions, with agreement ranging from 72% to 100%; 29 resulted in recommendations for clinical practice and 2 were identified as requiring further research. Question 47, which addressed the definition of PJI, was reported separately. Humeral component loosening, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and C-reactive protein (CRP) were supported as components of the diagnostic criteria, whereas cloudy fluid, postoperative stiffness, serum WBC count, and D-dimer were not supported as independent criteria. Arthroscopic tissue biopsy, frozen section, and selective ultrasound-guided aspiration or synovial biopsy were supported as adjuncts to diagnosis. Five intraoperative tissue specimens, prolonged aerobic and anaerobic culture incubation, and routine perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis were supported. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) and synovial neutrophil testing were supported as adjuncts; alpha-defensin was considered potentially useful but insufficiently validated for formal inclusion; and leukocyte esterase inclusion was not recommended. Routine use of bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), or positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) was not supported. Evidence remained insufficient to determine the clinical significance of polymicrobial molecular results or routine negative control samples. Conclusion The 2025 ICM provides a consensus framework for the diagnosis of shoulder PJI, identifying several measures that can be incorporated into current clinical practice. However, substantial uncertainty remains because most recommendations are supported by limited evidence and several diagnostic tests lack sufficient sensitivity. Prospective, shoulder-specific studies are needed to define diagnostic thresholds and determine the role of emerging molecular, biomarker, and imaging modalities.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of the Resisted Anterior Drawer (RAD) Test for Lateral Elbow Instability in Lateral Epicondylitis.
abstract: Background Lateral epicondylitis (LE) is increasingly recognized as a multifactorial condition in which subtle lateral elbow instability may contribute to persistent pain. However, reliable clinical tests to detect such instability are lacking. Purpose To determine the diagnostic accuracy of the resisted anterior drawer (RAD) test for detecting lateral elbow instability in patients with LE. Methods Consecutive adult patients diagnosed with LE underwent standardized clinical examination followed by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The RAD test was considered positive when pain during resisted wrist extension, with the elbow in extension, decreased by at least 1 point on a visual analogue scale (VAS) with anteromedial stabilization of the radial head. MRI-defined instability was defined as the presence of lateral collateral ligament (LCL) injury, posterior sagging, or ulnohumeral joint-line opening of grade ≥1. Diagnostic indices were calculated with 95% confidence intervals and likelihood ratios, and the continuous reduction in pain was evaluated with receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Results A total of 500 elbows were analyzed (mean age: 51 years). MRI evidence of instability was present in 57.4% of elbows. The RAD test demonstrated a sensitivity of 95.8% (95% CI 92.8-97.6%), specificity of 82.2% (95% CI 76.5-86.7%), and overall accuracy of 90.0% (95% CI 87.1-92.3%), with positive and negative likelihood ratios of 5.4 and 0.05. The area under the ROC curve for the reduction in pain was 0.92 (95% CI 0.90-0.95). The magnitude of pain reduction during the RAD maneuver correlated with the severity of MRI-defined instability (Spearman ρ = -0.71). Increasing MRI severity was associated with a higher number of corticosteroid infiltrations, whereas symptom duration showed only a weak association with structural instability. Conclusion In this Level III diagnostic study, the RAD test showed high sensitivity and good specificity for MRI-defined lateral elbow instability in patients with LE, and the magnitude of pain reduction was correlated with MRI-defined severity. These findings suggest that the RAD test may be a useful screening maneuver for instability-related pain in patients with LE. A prospective, blinded cohort study with an independent reference standard is required to confirm its clinical utility. Level of evidence Level III, Diagnostic Study.

title: Functional outcomes over 24 months after arthroscopic repair of isolated subscapularis tendon tears in a multicentre study.
abstract: Background Isolated subscapularis tears are rare, and it is currently unclear how the tear size relates to the postoperative outcomes after arthroscopic repair. This study aimed to evaluate clinical- and patient-reported outcomes, as well as adverse events of arthroscopically treated isolated subscapularis tears based on the tear extent over 24 months. Methods Across 19 orthopaedic centres, 69 patients undergoing primary arthroscopic repair for isolated subscapularis tears were prospectively recruited between June 2020 and November 2021. Medical imaging examinations were conducted at baseline and at 12 months. Clinical- and patient-reported outcomes were obtained at baseline, 6, 12, and 24 months. Adverse events within 24 months were documented. Patients were grouped into partial tears (n = 14), full-thickness tears of the superior half (n = 35) or complete full-thickness tears (n = 20) of the subscapularis. All outcomes were compared using generalised linear mixed models adjusted for baseline values, age, sex, American Society of Anaesthesiologists classification, tear aetiology, and steroid infiltrations. Results Improvements in all outcome scores were observed after surgery. No group differences were observed in the ranges of motion in flexion, abduction and external rotation (P≥0.634). The partial tear group had a higher pain level than both full-thickness groups at 12 months (P≤0.005). Abduction strength, Constant Score, Oxford Shoulder Score, Subjective Shoulder Value and EQ-5D-5L showed positive changes within 12- or 24-month follow-ups, with no group differences (P≥0.089). The risk of at least a symptomatic adverse event of any severity level affecting the operated shoulder and arm was highest for patients with partial tears (50%) and lowest for patients with complete full-thickness tears (25%). The most frequent occurrences were persistent or worsening pain, stiffness, and recurrent defects. Overall, 62% of patients with partial tears, 97% of patients with superior full-thickness tears and 77% of patients with complete full-thickness tears were satisfied at 24 months. Conclusion Arthroscopic repair of isolated subscapularis tears leads to significant and sustained improvements in clinical and patient-reported outcomes over 24 months, regardless of tear extent. However, patients with partial tears demonstrated greater residual pain and fewer patients reported satisfaction compared with those with full-thickness tears. These findings may reflect differences in patient characteristics and surgical treatment choices. Further studies are needed to determine the suitability and efficacy of surgical treatments for isolated subscapularis partial tears. Level of evidence Level III, Retrospective Cohort Comparison, Prognosis Study.

title: Surgical Treatment of Trans-ulnar Basal Coronoid Fracture-Dislocations: Clinical and Radiographic Outcomes in 34 Patients at a Mean 4-Year Follow-up.
abstract: Background Trans-ulnar basal coronoid (TUBC) fracture-dislocations represent a highly unstable pattern of elbow injury, characterized by a fracture through the base of the coronoid process that separates it from both the olecranon and the ulnar metaphysis. In TUBC fracture-dislocations, anatomic reduction and stable fixation of the coronoid are critical for restoring elbow function. The purpose of the present study was to evaluate the clinical and radiographic outcomes of patients surgically treated for TUBC fracture-dislocations. We analyzed fracture morphology, associated lesions, surgical approaches, coronoid fixation techniques, complications, and potential prognostic factors associated with inferior clinical outcomes. Materials and methods A retrospective review was performed of all patients surgically treated for TUBC fracture-dislocations at a single institution between 2012 and 2025 with a minimum clinical and radiographic follow-up of 12 months. Preoperative computed tomography scans were assessed to characterize fracture morphology and associated lesions. Clinical evaluation included elbow range of motion, Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS), Broberg and Morrey (B&M) score, QuickDASH, and Single Assessment Numeric Evaluation (SANE). Radiographs were reviewed to assess fracture healing and radiographic complications. Results Thirty-four patients were included, with a mean age of 51.8 years. Mean clinical and radiographic follow-up were 48 and 43.1 months, respectively. A radial head fracture was present in 28 patients. At final follow-up, mean elbow flexion-extension arc was 117.2°. Mean forearm rotation arc was 154.2°. Mean MEPS and B&M scores were 92.3 and 90.5 points, respectively, whereas mean QuickDASH and SANE scores were 14.8 and 85.6 points, respectively. Coronoid comminution (≥ 3 fragments) was associated with higher odds of a non-excellent MEPS (<90 points). Union of the proximal ulna was achieved in all cases; 2 cases of asymptomatic coronoid tip nonunion, and 2 cases of asymptomatic coronoid plate breakage were observed. Overall, 21 complications in 15 patients (44.1%) were recorded; 5 revision surgeries in 4 patients (11.8%) were performed. Conclusions TUBC fracture-dislocations are complex injuries characterized by substantial variability in fracture morphology, in which accurate reduction and stable fixation of the coronoid are considered essential for achieving favorable outcomes. Most patients in the present series achieved satisfactory functional outcomes, with good or excellent MEPS results in more than 90% of cases. However, the overall complication rate remained substantial (44.1%) with a reoperation rate of 11.8%. originalAbstract:
Background

Trans-ulnar basal coronoid (TUBC) fracture-dislocations represent a highly unstable pattern of elbow injury, characterized by a fracture through the base of the coronoid process that separates it from both the olecranon and the ulnar metaphysis. In TUBC fracture-dislocations, anatomic reduction and stable fixation of the coronoid are critical for restoring elbow function. The purpose of the present study was to evaluate the clinical and radiographic outcomes of patients surgically treated for TUBC fracture-dislocations. We analyzed fracture morphology, associated lesions, surgical approaches, coronoid fixation techniques, complications, and potential prognostic factors associated with inferior clinical outcomes.

Materials and methods

A retrospective review was performed of all patients surgically treated for TUBC fracture-dislocations at a single institution between 2012 and 2025 with a minimum clinical and radiographic follow-up of 12 months. Preoperative computed tomography scans were assessed to characterize fracture morphology and associated lesions. Clinical evaluation included elbow range of motion, Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS), Broberg and Morrey (B&M) score, QuickDASH, and Single Assessment Numeric Evaluation (SANE). Radiographs were reviewed to assess fracture healing and radiographic complications.

Results

Thirty-four patients were included, with a mean age of 51.8 years. Mean clinical and radiographic follow-up were 48 and 43.1 months, respectively. A radial head fracture was present in 28 patients. At final follow-up, mean elbow flexion-extension arc was 117.2°. Mean forearm rotation arc was 154.2°. Mean MEPS and B&M scores were 92.3 and 90.5 points, respectively, whereas mean QuickDASH and SANE scores were 14.8 and 85.6 points, respectively. Coronoid comminution (≥ 3 fragments) was associated with higher odds of a non-excellent MEPS (<90 points). Union of the proximal ulna was achieved in all cases; 2 cases of asymptomatic coronoid tip nonunion, and 2 cases of asymptomatic coronoid plate breakage were observed. Overall, 21 complications in 15 patients (44.1%) were recorded; 5 revision surgeries in 4 patients (11.8%) were performed.

Conclusions

TUBC fracture-dislocations are complex injuries characterized by substantial variability in fracture morphology, in which accurate reduction and stable fixation of the coronoid are considered essential for achieving favorable outcomes. Most patients in the present series achieved satisfactory functional outcomes, with good or excellent MEPS results in more than 90% of cases. However, the overall complication rate remained substantial (44.1%) with a reoperation rate of 11.8%. A key finding of this study was that coronoid comminution was associated with poorer functional outcomes and higher odds of non-excellent MEPS results.

title: CT-Based Morphology and Outcomes After ORIF of Humeral Head Articular Fractures.
abstract: Background Articular fractures of the humeral head encompass a spectrum of injuries. CT-based assessment of the extent of articular injury may influence reduction, functional outcomes, and avascular necrosis (AVN), but its association with outcomes after open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) remains incompletely understood. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 109 patients with humeral head articular fractures treated between 2010 and 2023 and classified fractures into five types using preoperative CT. Outcomes were analysed in 78 patients undergoing ORIF (mean age, 43 years; range, 20-68; SD, 11). Functional scores, reduction quality, and AVN incidence were compared across fracture types; complications and reoperations were recorded. Age and sex adjusted Constant scores (CS) and QuickDASH scores were assessed at a mean follow-up of 62 months (range, 24-122; SD, 18) after index ORIF. Exploratory multivariable analyses evaluated associations between fracture type and functional outcomes after adjustment for selected patient and injury characteristics. Reduction quality was graded as anatomical, acceptable, or poor using predefined radiographic criteria. Post-arthroplasty functional outcomes were analysed separately. Results Union was achieved in 72 of 78 patients (92%). Mean CS was 69 (range, 28-100; SD, 18) and mean QuickDASH was 29 (range, 2.3-61.4; SD, 14). Functional outcomes differed among fracture types (CS and QuickDASH, both p < 0.001), with poorer function in types 3-5. These associations persisted after adjustment for tuberosity involvement and articular fragment dislocation, with additional adjustment for age and sex for the QuickDASH model (p < 0.001 for both CS and QuickDASH). Anatomical reduction was more frequent in types 1 and 2 than types 3- 5 (p = 0.018). AVN developed in 14 patients (18%), exclusively in types 3-5 (p = 0.015). 12 (15%) patients underwent conversion arthroplasty after failed ORIF. At a mean of 21 months after salvage arthroplasty, significant improvements were observed in CS (mean increase, 23.7 points, p < 0.001) and QuickDASH scores (mean decrease, 21.4 points, p < 0.001) CONCLUSIONS: Most humeral head articular fractures healed after ORIF with acceptable clinical outcomes. Fractures with complete articular separation, comminution, and associated articular impaction, were associated with less frequent anatomical reduction, more AVN, and poorer shoulder and upper limb function. CT-based characterization may facilitate assessment of the extent of articular injury and its association with outcomes, although independent validation is required. Level of evidence Level III, Retrospective Cohort Comparison, Prognosis Study.

title: Subscapularis Healing and the Associated Impact on Outcomes Following Reverse Shoulder Arthroplasty.
abstract: Background The role of subscapularis repair following reverse shoulder arthroplasty (rTSA) remains controversial, particularly regarding restoration of internal rotation and postoperative function. While prior studies have compared repair versus non-repair, few have evaluated postoperative tendon integrity using ultrasound. Without direct assessment of tendon healing, functional differences cannot be reliably attributed to repair status. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the relationship between subscapularis healing and clinical outcomes following rTSA. Methods A retrospective review of prospectively collected data was performed of patients undergoing primary lateralized rTSA from 2022-2025 by a single surgeon. Patients underwent subscapularis repair with optional augmentation. Subscapularis repair was classified as healed or non-healed based on ultrasound evaluation at minimum 10-weeks. Patients with at least 1-year follow-up and postoperative ultrasound evaluation of the subscapularis were included. Patients with preoperative fractures or full-thickness subscapularis tears were excluded. Outcomes included VAS pain score, ASES score, SST score, range of motion, strength testing, and complication rates. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the association between augmentation and healing, adjusting for ultrasound timing and sex. Multivariable linear regression assessed the association between healing and postoperative ROM at 12 and 24 months, adjusting for preoperative motion and posterosuperior rotator cuff integrity. Significance was set at p < 0.05. Results Of 235 patients who underwent subscapularis repair, 126 shoulders (118 patients) met inclusion criteria. Healing was observed in 100 patients (79.4%). Healed repairs were significantly associated with augmentation (84.9% vs. 67.5%, p = .025), however, this association was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for ultrasound timing and sex (p = .113). Healed tendons demonstrated lower VAS pain (0 vs 1, p = 0.014) and ASES scores at 24 months (92 vs. 85, p = .022), though these differences are below the MCID. Internal rotation was improved at 12 months (6 vs. 4, p = 0.017). Healing was not independently associated with forward elevation, abduction, external rotation, or internal rotation at 12 or 24 months after multivariable adjustment. Complications occurred in 7.0% of patients with healed repairs and none with non-healed repairs (p = .343). Conclusion Sonographically intact subscapularis repairs following lateralized rTSA were associated with greater internal rotation at 1-year, however it was not independently associated with postoperative ROM after adjustment. This study represents one of the largest cohorts of sonographically evaluated subscapularis repairs following RTSA. Further investigation of biologic augmentation strategies may help improve subscapularis repair outcomes in rTSA. Level of evidence Level III; Retrospective Cohort Comparison; Prognosis Study.

title: A Preliminary Study of MRI with Zero Echo Time Sequence for Combined Fracture and Rotator Cuff Assessment in Proximal Humerus Fractures.
abstract: Background Proximal humerus fractures (PHF) are common in the elderly population, and accurate fracture characterization is essential for treatment planning. Computed tomography (CT) improves fracture visualization; however, radiation exposure and shortcomings in soft-tissue evaluation are its main disadvantages. Magnetic resonance imaging with ZTE sequence (ZTE MRI) enables CT-like imaging and enhances bone imaging while simultaneously allowing for the evaluation of soft tissues using standard sequences, all without radiation exposure. We hypothesized that ZTE MRI would demonstrate diagnostic performance comparable to CT in the classification of PHF, while also offering the added value of soft-tissue assessment. Methods This retrospective comparative study included patients with PHF who underwent shoulder MRI with a ZTE sequence within 21 days after CT. Two independent observers (orthopedic surgeon, radiologist) evaluated anonymized CT and ZTE MRI datasets in separate sessions for Neer fracture type, articular extensions, fracture dislocations and glenoid fractures with a two-week period between modalities. Standard MRI sequences were reviewed to identify concomitant rotator cuff and long head of biceps tendon injuries. Intra- and interobserver agreement was assessed using Cohen's kappa and intraclass correlation coefficients. Results Thirty-six patients met the inclusion criteria. ZTE MRI demonstrated very good agreement with CT for Neer classification (κ = 0.840, p < 0.001). Interobserver agreement ranged from 0.52-0.80 on CT and 0.46-0.72 on ZTE MRI. Intraobserver agreement was high for both observers, ranging 0.70-0.90 on CT and 0.68-0.88 on ZTE MRI. The highest reproducibility was observed for the humeral head, greater tubercle, and surgical neck fracture components. Conventional MRI sequences identified full-thickness rotator cuff tears in 12 of 36 patients (33.3%), including patients with minimally displaced fractures. Conclusion ZTE MRI provides fracture assessment comparable to CT, with similar intra- and interobserver reliability across major fracture components. Beyond matching CT performance in PHF characterization, ZTE MRI offers the significant advantages of radiation-free imaging and simultaneous assessment of full-thickness rotator cuff tears using conventional MRI sequences. These preliminary findings suggest that ZTE MRI may serve as a reliable alternative to CT in the initial evaluation of PHF, particularly when a comprehensive assessment of both bone and soft tissue is desired. Larger prospective studies are needed to validate the clinical impact of these observations.

title: Bone Density Measures in Preoperative CT Scans reflect Mechanical Bone Properties in Shoulder Arthroplasty Patients: Validation of Preoperative Bone Quality Predictions.
abstract: Bone quality critically affects fixation and complications in shoulder arthroplasty, yet routine preoperative computed tomography (CT) attenuation is rarely converted to quantitative bone mineral density (BMD) for preoperative planning. We hypothesized that phantomless, patient-specific calibrated preoperative CT with three-dimensional (3D) epiphyseal regions of interest (ROIs) reflects the mechanical properties of cancellous humeral bone in shoulder arthroplasty patients. Two cohorts underwent the same preoperative CT workflow: a multicenter clinical cohort (n = 242) establishing baseline characteristics and a bicentric validation cohort (n = 57) enabling mechanical testing. CT Hounsfield Unit (HU) values were internally calibrated using air-muscle-fat references and mapped to mgHA/cm3. An automated script extracted epiphyseal cylindrical ROIs to compute volumetric bone mineral density (BMD) and bone volume fraction (BV/TV). In the validation cohort, from resected humeral heads in arthroplasty procedures, trabecular cylinders (10 mm diameter; 12-18 mm length; aspect ratio > 1) were cored along the anatomical metaphyseal axis, embedded along the cylinder axis between stainless-steel endcaps, and tested in uniaxial compression after preconditioning to obtain yield strength and compression modulus. In the validation cohort, mean yield strength was 3.21 ± 1.35 MPa (95% CI 0.57-6.82) and compression modulus was 73.0 ± 38.3 MPa (95% CI 9.1-143.9). Epiphyseal CT-BMD correlated with yield strength (r = 0.67, R2 = 0.45, p < 0.0001) and compression modulus (r = 0.60, R2 = 0.36, p < 0.0001); BV/TV showed similar associations (yield strength r = 0.64, R2 = 0.41; compression modulus r = 0.65, R2 = 0.42; all p < 0.001). Mechanical properties reflected preoperative density discrimination: low vs. high density clusters demonstrated significant differences in yield strength 2.50 ± 1.04 vs. 4.00 ± 1.22 MPa (p < 0.001) and compression modulus 56.7 ± 29.6 vs. 93.4 ± 38.8 MPa (p = 0.0002). Phantomless, patient-specific calibrated preoperative CT with 3D epiphyseal ROIs reflects humeral cancellous mechanical properties and stratifies bone quality; integrating this workflow into planning could potentially optimize implant fixation decisions and reduce complication risk. title: Association of Respiratory-Related Sarcopenia Classification With Postoperative Complications and Overall Survival in Older Patients With Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma.
abstract: Introduction Respiratory function and muscle measures have previously been studied together. We evaluated a classification combining peak expiratory flow and a computed tomography-derived pectoralis muscle index in older patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Methods This retrospective cohort included 742 patients aged ≥65 y undergoing minimally invasive McKeown esophagectomy during 2020-2021. Pectoralis muscle index was the bilateral pectoralis major area at T4 divided by height squared, a surrogate of chest-wall muscle reserve. Two isolated-abnormality phenotypes were combined exploratorily into mild, alongside normal and severe categories. Logistic and Cox regression evaluated associations. Survival discrimination was assessed in the development cohort; stratified Cox sensitivity analyses addressed nonproportional hazards. Results Normal, mild, and severe comprised 340, 310, and 92 patients. Adjusted pneumonia odds ratios versus normal were 1.548 (95% confidence interval, 1.039-2.306) for mild and 2.973 (1.746-5.064) for severe. The leakage model retained no other covariates. In the T/N-stratified survival model, hazard ratios were 2.445 (1.948-3.067) and 3.585 (2.618-4.908), respectively. Adding the classification increased the apparent C-index from 0.837 to 0.861. Pneumonia areas under the curve were 0.616 for the four-group framework and 0.613 for the simplified classification. Conclusions The classification was associated with postoperative outcomes and overall survival. Its simpler grouping had observed discrimination close to the four-group framework. However, its clinical utility in preoperative optimization still requires further validation in prospective studies.

title: Strategies for Portal Vein Anastomosis in Pediatric Liver Transplantation: Hemodynamic Analysis.
abstract: Introduction Pediatric liver transplantation is the optimal treatment for children with end-stage liver disease. However, using adult donor livers often leads to portal vein size mismatch, increasing anastomotic risks. Hemodynamic assessment is crucial for surgical success. Methods Numerical simulations using non-Newtonian fluid models were performed to compare normal portal vein anatomy, three hypoplastic models, and five anastomotic types. Key parameters included flow distribution, velocity, pressure, and wall shear stress (WSS). Simulated flow rates were validated against published clinical data. Results Stenosis increased flow velocity and pressure. The 50% stenosis model reached a WSS of 35 Pa-three times the normal value-with high stress zones near the bifurcation. Certain anastomotic techniques improved hemodynamic performance. Conclusions Confluence and interposition graft anastomoses most closely restored normal hemodynamics. Optimal reconstruction requires not only sufficient diameter but also geometric continuity, axial alignment, and attention to bifurcation walls to avoid complications. Clinical validation with intraoperative flow probes and postoperative ultrasound is needed. Additional simulations augmented inflow conditions (simulating collateral ligation) demonstrate that increased inflow elevates WSS by 28%-35% at the bifurcation outer wall in geometrically suboptimal anastomoses, supporting the selective use of augmentation maneuvers.

title: Outcomes of Surgery After Neoadjuvant Chemoimmunotherapy in Selected N3 Stage III Non-small cell lung cancer: A Propensity Score-Matched Analysis.
abstract: Background While the conversion of unresectable stage III non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) to resectable status is a growing area of research, few studies have delineated the prognosis of clinical N3 patients undergoing surgery after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy. This retrospective study compared the outcomes of stage III patients with NSCLC at clinical N3 who successfully underwent surgical resection after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy with those of stage III N0-2 patients who received the same treatment followed by surgery in a matched cohort. Methods Drawing from a database of patients with NSCLC at Shanghai Pulmonary Hospital (2019-2023), we identified individuals with clinical Stage III (N3) disease, as well as those with Stage III (N0-2) disease, who underwent surgical resection following neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy. For these patients, after completion of neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy, mandatory re-biopsy of the originally involved N3 stations (via EBUS-TBNA or supraclavicular puncture) was required to confirm pathological negativity before surgical resection was subsequently performed only for cases validated as resectable by a multi-disciplinary team assessment. We utilized 3:1 propensity score matching to adjust for baseline imbalances between the study cohorts. The primary outcome was Disease-Free Survival (DFS). Results In the matched cohort, 57 patients with clinical Stage III (N3) NSCLC and 171 paired patients with clinical Stage III (N0-2) analysis showed that the objective response rate (ORR) was 62.2% in the N3 cohort and 69.1% in the N0-2 cohort. Additionally, the 3-year DFS rates were 67.2% vs 73.3% (hazard ratio = 1.37; 95% confidence interval = 0.76-2.49, P= .29). Further subgroup analysis revealed that the DFS rates of 22 patients with Biopsy-confirmed cN3 disease and 35 patients with PET/CT-confirmed cN3 disease were similar, and the 3-year DFS rates were 59.3% vs 72.2% (hazard ratio = 1.43; 95% confidence interval = 0.56-3.64, P = .45). Multivariate analysis suggested that pathological complete response (pCR) was an independent predictor of DFS prolongation in the N3 cohort. Conclusions For carefully selected patients with stage III (N3) NSCLC who achieve downstaging and undergo surgery after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy, postoperative DFS is comparable to that of N0-2 patients, supporting surgical intervention as a component of multimodal therapy in this specific subset of patients who achieve surgical conversion.

title: Low-dose CT Screening and Smoking Cessation: Separate and Joint Associations with Mortality among Ever-Smokers Eligible for Lung Cancer Screening.
abstract: Background Smoking cessation intervention is increasingly recognized as a core component of high-quality lung cancer screening (LCS). However, real-world evidence that compares the health effects of low-dose CT (LDCT) screening, smoking cessation, and their combination among screening-eligible current smokers remains limited. Methods We conducted a post-hoc analysis of data of the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST), defining recent quitting as smoking cessation within 2 years before enrolment as a proxy for cessation occurring close to screening initiation. Cox proportional hazards models were used to quantify associations of screening allocation and smoking cessation with LC-specific and all-cause mortality. Results Among 31,560 continuous smokers and recent quitters included in the analysis, 7,197 (22.8%) died from any cause during a median follow-up of 12.3 years. Of 30,915 participants included in cause-specific analyses, 1,783 (5.8%) died from LC. Among current smokers eligible for LCS, LDCT was associated with 12% lower LC mortality than chest radiography (CXR) (HR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.79-0.97), but no significant reduction of all-cause mortality (HR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.93-1.03). In the CXR arm, recent quitting was associated with substantially lower LC and all-cause mortality than continued smoking (HRs, 0.62 and 0.68; 95% CIs, 0.51-0.76 and 0.62-0.75, respectively), with similar reductions observed among recent quitters in the LDCT arm. Conclusions For screening-eligible current smokers, recent quitting was associated with substantially larger reductions in LC and all-cause mortality than those associated with LDCT screening. These findings reinforce the importance of integrating effective smoking cessation interventions into LCS programs.

title: Radiomics-Based Prediction of Post-TACE Milan Criteria Status and Survival Outcomes in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Retrospective Machine Learning Study.
abstract: Purpose To develop and evaluate machine learning models integrating radiomic features from pre- and post-transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) CT and MRI with clinical variables to predict 6-month Milan criteria status, overall survival (OS), and time to progression (TTP) in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Materials and methods This retrospective single-center study included 428 treatment-naive patients with biopsy-confirmed HCC who underwent conventional TACE (2010-2025) with post-TACE CT, pre- and post-TACE MRI, and 6-month imaging follow-up. nnU-Net segmented CT (liver, lipiodol, tumor) and MRI (liver, tumor) compartments, and radiomic features were extracted. Five feature configurations (shape and first-order features, alone and with clinical variables, and both combined with clinical variables) were evaluated. AutoGluon predicted 6-month Milan status, evaluated by repeated 5×5 cross-validation (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC]) and compared with clinical-only and baseline-Milan reference models; OS and TTP were assessed by concordance index (C-index) with leakage-corrected repeated cross-validation. Results Cross-validated Milan AUCs were 0.766-0.791 for radiomic configurations, exceeding a clinical-only model (0.711) but not baseline Milan status alone (0.842); adding shape features to clinical variables and baseline Milan status did not improve discrimination (0.874 vs 0.865; P = .43). Shape features with clinical variables had the numerically highest C-index for OS (0.647) and TTP (0.571), without improvement over clinical-only models. Conclusion Shape descriptors carried most of the imaging signal for 6-month Milan status, adding discrimination beyond clinical variables but not beyond baseline Milan status; survival discrimination was modest (OS) to near chance (TTP).

title: Acoustic Correlates of Endoscopically Identified Vocal Fold Lesions in a Large Clinical Cohort: Perceptual Associations and Screening Performance.
abstract: Benign vocal fold lesions are among the most common causes of dysphonia, yet large cohort studies integrating endoscopic, perceptual, and acoustic domains remain scarce. This study aimed to determine the prevalence and distribution of vocal fold lesions in a large clinical cohort and to determine acoustic characteristics linked to endoscopically detected vocal fold lesions and able to differentiate them from structurally normal vocal folds, corroborated by perceptual severity ratings. Methods In this cross-sectional cohort study, 782 patients with dysphonia underwent videolaryngostroboscopy, standardized acoustic recording, and auditory-perceptual evaluation using the Consensus Auditory-Perceptual Evaluation of Voice (CAPE-V) and GRBAS scales. Acoustic parameters (jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio [HNR], and smoothed cepstral peak prominence [CPPS]) were compared across lesion categories and entered into multivariable logistic regression models. Results Vocal fold polyps were the most prevalent lesion (32.1%), followed by nodules (24.0%), Reinke's edema (16.0%), cysts (13.9%), and granuloma (7.9%). All acoustic parameters differed significantly across categories (P < .001), with polyps showing the greatest deviation from normal values. CPPS was the strongest independent predictor of lesion presence (adjusted OR 1.62 per 1-dB decrease, P < .001) and correlated most strongly with CAPE-V overall severity (r = -.71, P < .001). The combined acoustic model discriminated lesion from non-lesion voices with excellent accuracy (AUC = 0.91). Conclusions Acoustic changes, such as decreased CPPS and HNR and increased jitter and shimmer, were related to vocal fold lesions identified by endoscopy. CPPS had the greatest separation between patients with a lesion, identified endoscopically, and structurally normal patients. These acoustic measures should be viewed as a screening/triage marker of vocal fold abnormality and not as a marker of benignity or lesion-specific etiology, however, because the study excluded malignant, neurological, and other major voice pathologies. Acoustic assessment is thus a useful non-invasive complement to laryngeal endoscopic assessment, but should not replace it.

title: Spasmodic Dysphonia and Muscle Tension Dysphonia: A Review of Neuroimaging and Neurophysiological Evidence.
abstract: Objectives Spasmodic dysphonia (SD), or laryngeal dystonia (LD), and muscle tension dysphonia (MTD) are clinically overlapping voice disorders with different positions in current pathophysiological models. This review synthesizes multimodal neuroimaging and neurophysiological evidence on their central mechanisms, compares the implicated neural systems, and assesses whether such measures can aid future differential diagnosis. Methods A structured search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Europe PMC, and Google Scholar (final search, March 29, 2026), limited to English-language publications from January 2000 through March 2026 and supplemented by reference-list screening and forward citation tracking. Evidence was synthesized across task-based and resting-state fMRI, structural MRI and morphometry, diffusion tensor and kurtosis imaging, PET, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and magnetoencephalography. Studies were appraised qualitatively for design, sample size, diagnostic phenotype, comparator groups, treatment or botulinum toxin washout status, findings, and limitations. Results The SD/LD literature provided relatively consistent evidence of abnormalities across distributed voice-control networks involving cortical, subcortical, cerebellar, and brainstem systems, recurring in primary sensorimotor cortex, supplementary and premotor regions, inferior frontal and parietal cortices, insula, putamen, thalamus, cerebellum, and their white-matter connections. Some abnormalities persisted outside phonation or before movement onset, supporting a trait-like component; TMS showed impaired cortical inhibition and a shortened cortical silent period (CSP) in SD/LD. The MTD evidence base remained limited, comprising one case-control task-fMRI study of ten women, one single-patient pre-/post-treatment fMRI study, and one TMS study with an MTD comparator. These findings suggested possible central involvement but did not establish a causal mechanism, a stable MTD-specific network, or the contributions of compensation, state-dependent effects, and phonatory effort; comparable CSP shortening was not reported in MTD. Conclusions SD/LD is best understood as a distributed disorder of central voice-control networks, whereas MTD appears to be a hyperfunctional voice disorder with plausible but incompletely characterized central influences. Unequal evidence volume should not be read as established biological divergence, and the "neurological" versus "non-neurological" distinction remains provisional. Imaging and physiological measures are not yet validated biomarkers, and CSP is only a candidate marker pending replication and validation. Larger, clinically stratified, harmonized multimodal head-to-head studies are needed, potentially integrating neural, physiological, acoustic, and clinical measures for reliable differential diagnosis.

title: Preoperative alignment-dependent coronal laxity persists after mechanically aligned total knee arthroplasty but not kinematically aligned total knee arthroplasty: a longitudinal stress radiographic study.
abstract: Background In mechanically aligned total knee arthroplasty (MA-TKA), postoperative coronal laxity has been reported to correlate with the severity of preoperative varus deformity. Whether kinematically aligned TKA (KA-TKA) modifies this relationship remains unknown. This study aimed to compare postoperative coronal laxity between MA-TKA and KA-TKA using longitudinal stress radiography, and to determine whether the association between the preoperative hip-knee-ankle angle (HKA) and postoperative coronal laxity differs between the two alignment strategies. Methods Patients who underwent primary TKA for osteoarthritis were divided into an MA-TKA group, in which a bi-cruciate stabilized implant was used, and a KA-TKA group, in which a medial stabilized implant was used. Propensity score matching based on age, sex, body mass index, and preoperative HKA yielded 31 knees per group. Varus and valgus stress radiographs were obtained in full extension using a Telos device at 2 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, and 1 year postoperatively. Spearman's rank correlation coefficients (ρ) between the preoperative HKA and postoperative stress angles were calculated separately for each group, and radiographic alignment parameters were compared between groups. Results In the MA-TKA group, significant negative correlations were observed between the preoperative HKA and postoperative stress varus angles at all time points (ρ = -0.655 to -0.395, all p < 0.05), whereas no significant correlations were identified in the KA-TKA group (all p > 0.05). Patients who underwent primary TKA for osteoarthritis were divided into an MA-TKA group, in which a bi-cruciate stabilized implant was used, and a KA-TKA group, in which a medial stabilized implant was used. title: Narrow intercondylar notch is associated with medial meniscal injury, including ramp lesions, in elite female footballers undergoing ACL reconstruction.
abstract: In elite female footballers, concomitant meniscal injury at the time of ACL rupture influences long-term joint prognosis. A narrow intercondylar notch is an established anatomical risk factor for ACL injury, but its association with compartment-specific meniscal damage remains uncharacterised. Retrospective secondary analysis of a prospectively maintained single-surgeon surgical database of 158 female footballers (Tegner 9; mean age 19.8 ± 5.1 years) undergoing primary ACL reconstruction with bone-patellar tendon-bone (BPTB) autograft (2017-2024; minimum 24-month follow-up). Notch morphology was classified intraoperatively by arthroscopic assessment, with preoperative MRI-based notch width index (NWI) used as a secondary, confirmatory measurement. Associations were assessed with Fisher's exact test (odds ratios [OR], 95% confidence intervals [CI]) and multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age and injury-to-surgery interval. Meniscal injury was identified in 71 patients (44.9%). A narrow notch (n = 32) was associated with higher meniscal injury prevalence (75.0% vs 36.8%; OR 5.15; 95% CI 2.14-12.41; p = 0.0001), with a selective effect on the medial compartment (OR 4.07; p = 0.001) but not the lateral (p = 0.100). Medial ramp lesions showed the strongest association (OR 6.98; 95% CI 1.84-26.51; p = 0.005). The narrow notch remained independently associated with increased odds after adjustment (medial injury adjusted OR 4.02, p = 0.001; ramp lesion age-adjusted OR 7.03, p = 0.004). In this Level IV, hypothesis-generating study, a narrow intercondylar notch was independently associated with increased odds of medial meniscal injury, particularly ramp lesions. Preoperative NWI quantification may support risk stratification and a lower threshold for targeted arthroscopic exploration of the medial compartment, pending prospective validation. IV.

title: MONKEY Challenge: Machine-learning for Optimal detection of iNflammatory cells in KidnEY transplant biopsies.
abstract: Purpose Accurate quantification of inflammatory cells in Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS)-stained kidney transplant biopsies is essential for Banff classification but remains subjective and labor-intensive. To address this, the MONKEY challenge benchmarked deep learning (DL) methods for automated detection of mononuclear leukocytes and their subtypes. Materials and methods A multicenter dataset of 118 biopsies with co-registered PAS and immunohistochemically restained slides, comprising over 131,000 annotated cells, was used. The algorithms were evaluated on hold-out validation and test set using Free-response Receiver Operating Characteristic (FROC) analysis, alongside precision, recall, and F1-scores. Results Across diverse architectures, performance converged, with the top models achieving F1-scores up to 0.75 for overall detection. Lymphocyte detection performed well (F1 up to 0.78), whereas monocyte detection remained more challenging (F1 up to 0.47). To explore the potential clinical applicability of automated inflammatory cell detection, the winning model was integrated with renal tissue segmentation models, enabling compartment-specific evaluation and quantitative assessment of Banff-related lesions. In an independent multicenter cohort of 180 kidney transplant biopsies, DL-derived quantitative measurements demonstrated strong correlations with consensus pathologist scoring for several inflammation-related Banff lesions, particularly total inflammation and interstitial inflammation. Conclusions This study establishes the first multicenter, PAS-based, IHC-validated benchmark for inflammatory cell detection and provides a clinically grounded resource to support the development of robust, generalizable AI systems for transplant pathology. Beyond benchmark performance, our extended tissue-specific analyses demonstrate that inflammatory cell detection on routine PAS slides can be anatomically contextualized and translated into quantitative measurements that align with conventional Banff lesion assessment, providing a foundation for future AI-assisted evaluation of kidney transplant biopsies.

title: Field-of-View Impact on Multiclass Tissue Segmentation: Systematic Analysis Across Structure Sizes and Multiple Cancer Types.
abstract: Purpose Patch-based deep learning in digital pathology requires selecting a field-of-view size, a choice usually made without systematic justification. Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, measuring 5-10 μm, depend on the surrounding tissue context for identification. We aimed to determine how field-of-view size affects multiclass segmentation of tissue structures of different sizes at a fixed resolution and to identify a size that balances accuracy and computational cost. Materials and methods An EfficientNet-B3 U-Net was trained on the PanopTILs breast cancer dataset (153 whole-slide images) across five field-of-view sizes (224×224 to 512×512 pixels; 112-256 μm) at 0.5 μm/pixel. Four tissue classes were segmented and evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation with patient-level splits. Resized-patch controls and a 0.25 μm/pixel series separated field-of-view effects from resolution effects. The trained model was then applied to bladder and colon cancer tissues, and its tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte detection was compared with pathologist review. Results Detection sensitivity showed a strong inverse correlation with structure size (Pearson r = -0.98, p = 0.016). From 224×224 to 512×512 pixels, tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte segmentation improved by 46.6% (Dice score: 0.309 to 0.453, p = 0.0003) and stromal segmentation by 24.7% (p = 0.0001), while large structures remained stable (+0.4%). Overall Dice score plateaued between 384×384 and 512×512 pixels. At a fixed 224×224-pixel input, enlarging the tissue area by downsampling reduced the Dice score. The 384×384 field-of-view achieved 94.5% of maximum performance with 6.07 billion multiply-accumulate operations per image, compared with 10.79 billion for 512×512. Cross-cancer validation yielded 92% accuracy in bladder and 88% in colon cancer (Cohen's kappa = 0.85 and 0.94). Conclusions Field-of-view fundamentally determines detection capability for size-specific tissue structures. Performance plateaued between 384×384 and 512×512 pixels, and the 384×384 field-of-view offers a favorable balance between performance and computational efficiency. The approach generalized to other cancer types without fine-tuning.
