title: Nonverbal reasoning in children and adolescents with cerebral palsy: associations with gross motor function, MRI, and EEG findings.
abstract: To examine the association between gross motor function level and Raven's Colored Progressive Matrices (CPM) performance in children and adolescents with cerebral palsy (CP), compare CPM performance with typically developing participants, and explore associations with MRI and EEG findings. This multicenter cross-sectional study included 40 participants with CP and 20 comparison participants aged 10-17 years. CPM totals were converted to center-derived age-referenced scores; the upper available normative age band was applied above age 11.5 years. Gross motor function was classified with the GMFCS. Clinically indicated MRI and EEG findings were categorized using prespecified systems. Median CPM score was 72 (IQR 64-81) in the CP group and 98 (IQR 92-104) in the comparison group (adjusted difference -26.4, 95% CI -31.2 to -21.6). GMFCS level was inversely associated with CPM score (Spearman rho = -.78, 95% CI -.85 to -.68). Predominant white matter injury was associated with lower CPM scores. The adjusted association with epileptiform EEG abnormalities was inconclusive. CPM performance was associated with GMFCS level and MRI pattern, but the cross-sectional findings do not establish causality. Gross motor classification must not substitute for accessible neuropsychological assessment.

title: Schizophrenia heterogeneity, treatment response to clozapine, and the Johns Hopkins Schizoaffective Disorders Precision Medicine Center of Excellence.
abstract: Schizophrenia heterogeneity has resisted resolution for over a century, with no unifying clinical feature, biomarker, or pathogenic pathway identified. This has produced imprecise diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment, while confounding mechanistic research. Prior subtyping approaches-based on clinical phenotype, longitudinal course, age of onset, neuroimaging, physiological measures, or etiological factors-have yielded partial insights but lack established clinical utility. The Johns Hopkins Schizoaffective Disorder Precision Medicine Center of Excellence (PMCOE) brings together patients and clinicians at the Johns Hopkins Hospital and the Johns Hopkins Bayview Community Psychiatry Program with Johns Hopkins schizophrenia investigators to address this heterogeneity through stratification by treatment response, dividing patients into non-treatment-resistant (nonTRS), clozapine-responsive treatment-resistant (crTRS), and ultra-treatment-resistant (uTRS) subgroups. The term "Schizoaffective Disorder" was chosen to include schizophrenia with varying degrees of affective symptomatology, deliberately creating a broadly inclusive patient group. We hypothesize that these subtypes reflect distinct pathophysiological processes and that identifying their biological correlates will improve clinical decision-making and reveal novel therapeutic targets. The PMCOE pursues this hypothesis across four aims. Aim 1 characterizes clinical, cognitive, functional, quality-of-life, and olfactory signatures distinguishing subtypes, with preliminary data showing worse cognition and function in uTRS versus crTRS, and a temporal sequence of clozapine benefit (symptoms, then function, then quality of life). Aim 2 applies 7T structural/functional MRI-including novel measures of microvascular perfusion (iVASO) and CSF clearance (cDSC)-alongside EEG-based dynamic causal and network modeling to probe excitatory/inhibitory imbalance across subtypes. Aim 3 investigates cellular and molecular mechanisms, particularly protein homeostasis dysfunction, using patient-derived induced neurons, organoids, and extracellular vesicles, with focused study of SCHEMA-identified risk genes, including CUL1. Aim 4 leverages electronic health record data to generate validated electronic phenotypes for treatment-response subtypes and to establish a learning health system translating findings into clinical practice. By anchoring subtyping to an empirically measurable, clinically actionable outcome, the PMCOE aims to accelerate biomarker discovery for clozapine response, clarify mechanisms of treatment resistance, and transform care for individuals with schizophrenia-particularly those with ultra-treatment-resistant illness, for whom therapeutic options remain critically limited.

title: Lung cancer multi-subtype classification via soft-voting ensemble architecture.
abstract: Lung cancer is a highly heterogeneous malignant tumour, and accurate classification of its subtypes is relevant to personalized treatment planning. However, overlapping imaging appearances and severe class imbalance make multi-subtype classification challenging. To address this problem, we propose a soft-voting ensemble of EfficientNet-B3, ConvNeXt-Tiny, and DenseNet-121. The three independently optimized backbones were selected for their complementary architectural characteristics and the framework does not explicitly disentangle or fuse their feature representations. Instead, it averages their class-probability outputs at inference. Experiments on a public dataset containing 18,500 CT-PET images show that the ensemble achieves an accuracy of 0.9865 and an F1 score of 0.9865. The class-wise recalls for adenocarcinoma, large cell carcinoma, small cell carcinoma, and squamous cell carcinoma are 99.55%, 100.00%, 96.17%, and 98.20%, respectively. These retrospective image-level results support further investigation of the framework as a potential radiologist-assistance tool.

title: Non-invasive vascular assessment in gestational hypertension and preeclampsia during pregnancy and the postpartum period: a systematic review.
abstract: Objective To evaluate evidence on non-invasive vascular assessment techniques used during pregnancy and/or the postpartum period to identify vascular abnormalities associated with gestational hypertension and explore potential implications for long-term cardiovascular health. Methods A systematic search of MEDLINE, PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Library, and gray literature (to May-2024) identified studies assessing vascular structure or function using pulse-wave velocity, carotid intima-media thickness, flow-mediated dilation, ophthalmic artery Doppler, and retinal imaging. Forty-nine studies involving 32,683 participants. Due to the heterogeneity in study design and methodology, findings were synthesized narratively. Results Women with gestational hypertension generally demonstrated increased arterial stiffness (elevated pulse wave velocity and augmentation index), impaired endothelial function (reduced flow-mediated dilation), and increased intima-media thickness during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Several studies reported persistence of these abnormalities from weeks to years after delivery, although findings were inconsistent. Ophthalmic artery Doppler studies showed variable alterations in peak systolic velocity ratios and pulsatility index reported in hypertensive pregnancies. Retinal imaging identified alterations in retinal vessel caliber during pregnancy and the postpartum period, with some abnormalities reported up to six years postpartum. Conclusion Non-invasive vascular assessments can help identify macrovascular, microvascular, and endothelial abnormalities in women with gestational hypertension and preeclampsia during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Although some abnormalities persist beyond delivery and may contribute to long-term cardiovascular risk, evidence remains insufficient to support their use as independent predictors of future cardiovascular events. Further standardized, prospective longitudinal studies are needed to determine their prognostic and clinical value.

title: Prehospital Trauma Compendium: Prehospital Management of Pediatric Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Circulatory Arrest - A Joint Position Statement and Resource Document of NAEMSP, ACS-COT, ACEP, and AAP.
abstract: In 2014 the National Association of EMS Physicians (NAEMSP), American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma (ACS-COT), American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP), and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) published the first joint position statement discussing withholding and discontinuing resuscitation attempts for pediatric traumatic out-of-hospital circulatory arrest (TOHCA). Since then, the body of literature addressing pediatric TOHCA has evolved and evidence has grown that demonstrates the nearly uniformly poor prognosis of children who suffer circulatory arrest in the prehospital setting as a result of trauma. To support emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians in their approach to these high-acuity, low-frequency, and challenging cases, this project aimed to update guidance regarding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts for pediatric traumatic circulatory arrest.NAEMSP, ACEP, ACS-COT, and AAP recommend:EMS resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA should:Prioritize prompt identification of patients who may benefit from transport to definitive care at trauma centers when safe and appropriate. On-scene resuscitation should be balanced against the potential benefit of transfer to a proximate trauma center.Emphasize the identification of reversible causes of traumatic circulatory arrest and timely use of clinically indicated life-saving interventions (LSIs) within the EMS clinician's scope of practice. These include:External hemorrhage control with direct pressure, wound packing, and tourniquetsAirway management using the least-invasive airway interventions required to achieve and maintain airway patency, oxygenation, and adequate ventilation.Chest decompression if clinical concern for tension pneumothorax. Empiric bilateral decompression is not recommended in the absence of suspected thoracic trauma.External chest compressions and ventilations have a larger role in pediatric TOHCA resuscitation than in adult TOHCA resuscitation, with children frequently having TOHCA secondary to head injury, hypoxia and other non-hemorrhagic mechanisms. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be provided when the cause of circulatory arrest is unclear.Epinephrine is of lower priority than other LSIs.Consider point of care ultrasound (POCUS) to guide decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts.Resuscitation attempts may be withheld in pediatric TOHCA patients with:Injuries that are incompatible with life (e.g., decapitation, hemi-corpectomy, incineration).Evidence of prolonged circulatory arrest (e.g., rigor mortis, dependent lividity, decomposition).Advanced care planning documents that indicate Do Not Resuscitate (DNR)/ Do Not Attempt Resuscitation (DNAR)/Allow Natural Death medical orders.Resuscitation attempts may be discontinued in pediatric TOHCA patients who:Have no return of spontaneous circulation after provision of at least 15 minutes of high-quality CPR in addition to performance of other lifesaving interventions directed at treating potentially reversible causes of pediatric TOHCA. Longer durations of CPR, up to 30 minutes, may be considered for patients with positive predictors of survival such as organized rhythm, witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, or with proximate access to a trauma center.Have known predictors of very low probability of survival such as penetrating trauma without proximate access to a trauma center, asystole, unwitnessed arrest, or lack of bystander CPR.Protocols guiding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA benefit from oversight by EMS physicians in collaboration with pediatric experts and local or regional trauma system stakeholders. Implementation of such protocols for pediatric patients benefits from involvement of community stakeholders including family representatives, law enforcement, medical examiner, and child fatality review committees.Considerations for protocol implementation include local resource availability, EMS clinician and public safety, psychosocial support to surviving family members and emergency responders, and dignified handling of the deceased patient.Training needs for EMS clinicians include techniques to communicate with family members regarding the death of a child and understanding the clinician's own response to this low-frequency, high-emotion experience.

title: Factors associated with mammography screening stages in Hispanic/Latina women in the USA: a transtheoretical model and health belief model approach.
abstract: Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths among Hispanic/Latina women in the U.S. and they are more likely to be diagnosed at later stages. Understanding psychosocial factors associated with mammography screening is important for addressing these disparities. This study examined associations between Transtheoretical Model (TTM) stages of mammography screening and constructs from the Health Belief Model (HBM) and TTM, including self-efficacy, perceived benefits, barriers, susceptibility, and seriousness, as well as family support, among Hispanic/Latina women aged 40 years and older in the U.S.A. A cross-sectional design using self-report surveys was employed, with 473 Hispanic/Latina women recruited through multiple nonprobability sampling strategies. A one-way ANCOVA compared psychosocial factors across the three combined TTM groups (precontemplation/contemplation/preparation, relapse/inconsistent, maintenance), controlling for age. Statistically significant differences were found among the three combined TTM groups for self-efficacy (F(2, 469) = 13.08, p = 0.000), benefits (F(2, 469) = 5.21, p = 0.006), barriers (F(2, 469) = 6.90, p = 0.001), susceptibility (F(2, 469) = 8.37, p = 0.000), seriousness (F(2, 469) = 4.64, p = 0.01), and family support (F(2, 469) = 10.34, p = 0.000). These significant differences across the three combined TTM groups highlight the multifaceted nature of mammography screening behavior. Family support, often underrepresented in traditional health behavior models, was also associated with the combined TTM groups. In this study, family support was primarily reflected in family-related health communication and advice. These findings suggest that using the HBM and TTM as complementary frameworks, alongside family support, may inform culturally tailored interventions addressing individual beliefs and familial contexts to promote regular mammography screening among Hispanic/Latina women. Future longitudinal research should examine these factors across Hispanic/Latina subgroups and settings to better understand their relationships with mammography screening and inform targeted health promotion strategies.

title: Efficacy of hysteroscopic curettage and niche resection in type II and III cesarean scar pregnancies.
abstract: Introduction To evaluate the efficacy and safety of hysteroscopic curettage combined with cesarean scar diverticulum canal-opening after focused ultrasound ablation surgery (FUAS) pretreatment in patients with type II and III cesarean scar pregnancy (CSP). Methods Clinical data of 105 patients with type II/III CSP treated between January 2019 and October 2022 were retrospectively analyzed. All patients received FUAS pretreatment. The observation group ( n = 47) underwent hysteroscopic curettage combined with niche canal-opening, while the control group ( n = 58) received hysteroscopic curettage alone. Surgical parameters, postoperative recovery, complications, reintervention rates, and menstrual outcomes were compared. Results The observation group had significantly shorter operation time [20 (15,25) vs. 25 (20,31) min, p = 0.001], less intraoperative blood loss [5 (5,10) vs. 10 (10,50) mL, p = 0.002], lower complication rate [4.3% vs. 17.2%, p = 0.038], and lower reintervention rate [4.3% vs. 19.0%, p = 0.023]. No between-group differences were observed in postoperative hemoglobin decline, hospital stay, vaginal bleeding duration, human chorionic gonadotropin normalization time, menstrual recovery time, or residual scar myometrial thickness (all p > 0.05). Among patients with preoperative prolonged menstruation, menstrual duration improved in both groups ( p < 0.05), with a higher improvement rate in the observation group [75.0% vs. 23.1%, p = 0.005]. Conclusions FUAS pretreatment combined with hysteroscopic surgery is safe and effective for type II/III CSP. Adding diverticulum canal-opening to hysteroscopic curettage further optimized surgical outcomes by reducing operation time, intraoperative blood loss, complication rates, and the need for reintervention, while also significantly improving prolonged menstruation. This combined strategy may serve as an optimized minimally invasive alternative for patients desiring fertility, though long-term reproductive safety requires further verification.

title: Diagnostic performance of MRI, endorectal ultrasound, and FAPI PET/MRI for identifying pathological complete response after short-course radiotherapy and chemoimmunotherapy in locally advanced rectal cancer: a retrospective study.
abstract: Background Accurate imaging-based response assessment is essential for proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC). This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of MRI, endorectal ultrasound (ERUS) and 18F-FAPI PET/MRI for identifying pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy (SCRT) followed by chemoimmunotherapy. Methods This single-center retrospective study included 143 patients. Diagnostic performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy with 95% confidence intervals. Cohen's κ assessed agreement between imaging-defined complete response (iCR) and pCR. Paired comparisons used Cochran's Q and Holm-adjusted exact McNemar tests. Results The pCR rate was 51.0%. MRI ( n = 118), ERUS ( n = 81), and PET/MRI ( n = 25) achieved sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 4.76%, 98.18%, and 48.31%; 30.95%, 87.18%, and 58.02%; and 60.0%, 100.0%, and 84.0%, respectively. PET/MRI-assessed imaging complete response showed substantial agreement with pCR (κ = 0.643). Conclusion Neoadjuvant SCRT followed by chemoimmunotherapy achieved high pCR rates in pMMR LARC. Conventional MRI and ERUS showed limited sensitivity despite relatively high specificity. 18F-FAPI PET/MRI showed potential diagnostic utility in a small subgroup, but its moderate sensitivity and limited sample size warrant further validation. These findings highlight the limitations of imaging alone and the need for comprehensive response assessment.

title: Combined radiofrequency electromagnetic and pulsed magnetic field exposure attenuates histological and molecular markers of acute colonic injury in young rats.
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease involves epithelial injury, ulceration, apoptosis, inflammation, and oxidative-stress dysregulation. Although bioelectromagnetic fields may modulate tissue responses, their effects on acute colitis remain unclear. This exploratory study assessed histological and molecular changes associated with combined radiofrequency electromagnetic field (RF-EMF) and pulsed magnetic field (PMF) exposure in acetic-acid-induced colitis.Thirty-two young female Wistar albino rats were allocated to Control, Colitis, Colitis+RF-EMF+PMF, or RF-EMF+PMF groups (n=8 each). Colitis was induced intrarectally with 4% acetic acid. Exposure comprised RF-EMF (27.12 MHz, 30 min/session, 12 cycles/day) and PMF (0.5 mT, continuous). After seven days, distal colonic specimens underwent semiquantitative histopathology, crypt morphometry, immunohistochemistry for CAS-3, IL-6, and TNF-α, and RT-qPCR for SIRT-1, NRF-2, and HO-1. Colitis caused histological injury, reduced crypt dimensions, increased CAS-3, IL-6, and TNF-α immunopositivity, and decreased SIRT-1, NRF-2, and HO-1 expression. Compared with untreated colitis, combined exposure increased crypt depth and width and reduced all three immunohistochemical markers (all Tukey-adjusted p<0.001). Overall histopathological injury was lower but not statistically significant (Dunn-adjusted p=0.068), whereas submucosal inflammatory infiltration decreased significantly (p=0.048). NRF-2 expression increased (Tukey-adjusted p=0.002); SIRT-1 and HO-1 increased numerically without statistical significance (p=0.057 and 0.134).Combined RF-EMF+PMF exposure was associated with preserved crypt architecture, reduced apoptotic and inflammatory immunopositivity, and increased NRF-2 expression. Absent barrier-function testing and incomplete RF dosimetry preclude conclusions regarding restored epithelial barrier function or established therapeutic efficacy.

title: Targeting Accelerated Aging in COPD: The AMICO (A Trial of Metformin In COpd) Trial Design.
abstract: Introduction Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is increasingly recognized as a disease of accelerated biological aging characterized by progressive lung function decline, emphysema progression and multiple age-related comorbidities. Current therapies improve symptoms and reduce exacerbations but have limited effects on disease progression. Metformin has demonstrated anti-aging properties through modulation of pathways involved in oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction and cellular senescence, making it a potential disease-modifying treatment in COPD. Methods AMICO (A Trial of Metformin In COPD) is an investigator-initiated, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial conducted in anonymous . A total of 212 patients with clinically stable COPD, centrilobular emphysema on computed tomography, post-bronchodilator FEV 1 40%-70% predicted and accelerated FEV 1 decline (>40 mL·year -1 ) will be randomized (1:1) to receive metformin (850 mg twice daily) or matching placebo for 36 months in addition to standard COPD treatment. Assessments include pulmonary function, chest computed tomography, exercise capacity, health status, muscle strength, body composition, age associated comorbidities development and aging-related biomarkers.The primary endpoint is the annual rate of FEV 1 decline over 36 months. Secondary endpoints include emphysema progression, changes in diffusing capacity, COPD Assessment Test score, 6-minute walk distance, BODE index, handgrip strength, exacerbations, major cardiovascular events, cancer incidence and renal dysfunction. Conclusions AMICO is the first randomized trial specifically designed to evaluate metformin as a gerotherapeutic and disease-modifying intervention in COPD. The study may provide novel evidence supporting geroscience-based approaches to slow disease progression and improve long-term outcomes in patients with COPD.

title: The FOXA2-BNIP3 axis alleviates acute necrotizing pancreatitis by promoting mitophagy in pancreatic acinar cells to inhibit mtDNA-mediated AIM2 inflammasome activation.
abstract: Acute necrotizing pancreatitis (ANP) is a severe inflammatory pancreatic disease characterized by pancreatic necrosis and systemic inflammation, with complex pathogenesis, rapid progression, and poor prognosis. Mitochondrial dysfunction in pancreatic acinar cells represents a pivotal early event in ANP; however, mitophagy, a central component of mitochondrial quality control, remains poorly characterized in terms of its role, regulatory networks, and therapeutic potential in ANP. In this study, we demonstrated that BNIP3 (BCL2 interacting protein 3) expression was significantly downregulated in patients with ANP and negatively correlated with inflammatory severity. Consistently, BNIP3-mediated mitophagy was impaired in the pancreatic tissue of ANP mouse models. Notably, restoration of BNIP3 expression using a novel adeno-associated virus targeting pancreatic tissue (AAV-PAN)- Bnip3 gene therapy vector alleviated pancreatic necrosis and systemic inflammatory injury, promoted mitophagy, and inhibited mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. Mechanistically, BNIP3-dependent mitophagy facilitated the clearance of damaged mitochondria and prevented mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release into the cytosol, thereby suppressing AIM2 (absent in melanoma 2) inflammasome activation and subsequent acinar cell pyroptosis. Furthermore, we identified the transcription factor FOXA2 (forkhead box A2) as a direct upstream regulator that bound to the Bnip3 promoter and positively regulated its expression. FOXA2 was downregulated in ANP, whereas pancreas-specific FOXA2 overexpression activated BNIP3-mediated mitophagy and conferred protection against inflammatory injury. Together, these findings uncovered a previously unrecognized mechanism whereby the FOXA2-BNIP3-AIM2 axis mitigated pancreatic and systemic inflammatory injury in ANP by enhancing mitophagy to restrain mtDNA-dependent AIM2 inflammasome activation, highlighting the FOXA2-BNIP3-AIM2 axis as a promising target for gene therapy. title: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Salmonella Typhi spondylodiscitis with vertebral collapse: a case report.
abstract: Introduction and importance Spondylodiscitis is an uncommon spinal infection that remains diagnostically challenging because of its non-specific symptoms and radiological overlap with tuberculosis and neoplasms. Among these, infections caused by Salmonella Typhi are extremely unusual, and the case becomes even more challenging when multidrug resistance (MDR) is present. Presentation of case We describe a 49-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension who presented with persistent back pain following an episode of enteric fever. Imaging showed spondylodiscitis with vertebral collapse, initially suspected as tuberculosis or metastasis. A mammogram and tuberculosis (TB) workup were negative. Definitive diagnosis was only achieved during surgery. Intraoperative biopsy and culture confirmed Salmonella Typhi , resistant to multiple antibiotics but sensitive to imipenem and azithromycin. Targeted therapy led to clinical improvement. Clinical discussion This case underlines the diagnostic difficulty of spinal infections, where radiology alone cannot differentiate between infection and malignancy. Surgical biopsy and culture remain essential, aligning with current Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommendations. Conclusion Multidrug-resistant Salmonella Typhi spondylodiscitis is exceptionally rare. Early tissue diagnosis and tailored therapy are key to achieving favorable outcomes.

We describe a 49-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension who presented with persistent back pain following an episode of enteric fever. title: Progression-free survival prediction in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: where can we further improve?
abstract: Introduction Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is a biologically heterogeneous disease in which approximately one-third of patients experience primary refractoriness or relapse despite modern chemoimmunotherapy. Although clinical prognostic indices remain the cornerstone of risk stratification, they incompletely capture the biological complexity underlying disease progression. Accurate prediction of progression-free survival (PFS) is essential to support personalized treatment strategies. Areas covered This review summarizes advances in PFS prediction in DLBCL, including clinical prognostic models, quantitative PET imaging, molecular and transcriptomic classification, genomic classifiers, tumor microenvironment profiling, circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA)-based biomarkers, and integrated multimodal prognostic models. Relevant literature was identified through PubMed, with ClinicalTrials.gov searched for ongoing clinical trials; searches were updated through 3 October 2026. We discuss the strengths, limitations, and clinical applicability of these approaches. Expert opinion Future prognostic models will increasingly rely on integrated multimodal frameworks combining clinical, imaging, molecular, immune, and dynamic response biomarkers. Among these, ctDNA has emerged as one of the most promising tools for measurable residual disease assessment. However, improving patient outcomes will require moving beyond prognostic accuracy toward predictive biomarkers capable of guiding personalized treatment selection across an evolving therapeutic landscape. Prospective validation, assay standardization, and demonstration of clinical utility will be essential for translating these approaches into routine practice.

title: Epiploic appendagitis: a review of diagnosis and treatment.
abstract: Introduction Epiploic Appendagitis (EA) is a rare, self-limiting cause of acute abdominal pain, often mistaken for conditions such as appendicitis or diverticulitis due to overlapping clinical presentations. We highlight four distinct instances of EA, emphasizing its diagnostic and therapeutic nuances. Areas covered We describe primary EA successfully managed conservatively with non-steroidal anti‑inflammatory drugs. We also describe EA with concomitant intra‑abdominal pathology requiring surgery (i.e. appendicitis) and managed conservatively with the EA (i.e cholecystitis). We further illustrate, with intraoperative and radiological imaging, the chronic sequelae of EA, a peritoneal loose body or a calcified epiploic appendage. These different types of presentations underscore the role of computed tomography as the gold-standard imaging modality for diagnosing epiploic appendagitis, characterized by hallmark findings (inflamed fat-density structures, the hyper-attenuating ring sign). Expert opinion By delineating primary and secondary EA, we aim to increase awareness among clinicians to distinguish this condition from other acute abdominal pathologies. Early recognition of EA and its benign course can prevent unnecessary surgical interventions, optimizing patient outcomes and reducing health care costs.

title: A Belgian study assessing relapsing multiple sclerosis activity through automated magnetic resonance imaging volumetry.
abstract: Aim This study assessed to what extent ico brain ms , a commercially available artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) volumetry software, detected disease activity in patients with clinically and radiologically stable relapsing multiple sclerosis (RMS), and estimated its impact on radiologists' assessments. Patients and methods We retrospectively enrolled 111 RMS patients with two consecutive MRI scans at one year interval, without relapses, progression or radiological changes while remaining on stable therapy. MRI scans were analyzed by four radiologists acting independently, and by ico brain ms . The radiologists performed their assessments both without and with ico brain ms support and categorized patient status based on lesion and brain volume changes. Results Radiologists' detection of lesion activity non-significantly increased from 6.8% to 8.6% (McNemar p = 0.215; ordinal regression p = 0.06; sign-test p = 0.08) using ico brain ms . Detection of accelerated brain volume loss increased from 2.0% to 7.7% (all p < 0.01). Inter-reader agreement improved from 36% to 56% for lesions, and from 26% to 40% for brain loss (Kendall's W, p < 0.001). Ico brain ms detected new or significantly enlarged lesions in 16.2% and accelerated brain volume loss in 6.3% of participants. Conclusion AI-assisted MRI volumetry may support radiologists to detect subclinical disease activity in patients characterized as having stable disease.

title: Effectiveness of a standardised cleaning protocol to prevent malignant cell contamination during EBUS-TBNA: Results from a European multicentre study.
abstract: Background Endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) and transoesophageal ultrasound with a bronchoscope (EUS-B) are key techniques for mediastinal staging in lung cancer. The 9th TNM classification underscores the prognostic importance of accurate station-specific nodal assessment. However, the optimal sampling strategy remains uncertain, particularly regarding needle reuse between N2 stations due to the risk of cross-contamination. Methods We conducted a prospective multicentre study including patients undergoing EBUS and/or EUS-B for diagnosis or staging of lung cancer or metastatic disease. A standardised transbronchial needle aspiration (TBNA) cleaning protocol was evaluated. The primary endpoint was the absence of malignant cells in post-cleaning needle rinse samples. Results Of 164 enrolled patients, 162 were included in the final analysis, comprising 270 sampled targets, with malignancy confirmed in 76.3%. The mean cleaning time was 148.8 ± 40.9 seconds per target, and the needle was visually assessed as clean in 89.3% of cases. Among malignant cases, post-cleaning needle rinse samples were negative for malignant cells in 92.2% and positive or suspicious in 7.8%. No clinical or procedural variables were associated with cleaning failure. Visual assessment of needle cleanliness did not correlate with cytological findings. No complications were observed. Conclusion A standardised needle-cleaning protocol is safe and effective in reducing malignant cell contamination during EBUS and EUS-B. However, residual contamination persists in a minority of cases, indicating that needle reuse may carry a small risk of cross-contamination between targets. This approach may represent a pragmatic alternative to routine needle exchange in clinical practice.

A standardised needle-cleaning protocol is safe and effective in reducing malignant cell contamination during EBUS and EUS-B. However, residual contamination persists in a minority of cases, indicating that needle reuse may carry a small risk of cross-contamination between targets. This approach may represent a pragmatic alternative to routine needle exchange in clinical practice.

title: Instance-specific brain image registration: learning deformable fields from a single image pair without external datasets.
abstract: Objective. To eliminate the reliance on large-scale external training datasets and achieve high-precision alignment for complex brain structures by overcoming the prevalent challenges of data scarcity and domain shifts in current deep learning-based registration methods. Approach. We propose a novel Instance-Specific Deep Brain Registration Framework that independently trains a dedicated model for each specific image pair. By reconceptualizing a single image pair as an internal dataset generator, we introduce a Multi-Scale Random Patch Learning strategy to construct a diverse local-to-global sample space. Architecturally, we design a Context-Aware Flow Predictor integrated with a Recurrent Context Transfer mechanism within a coarse-to-fine paradigm. Furthermore, a Topology-Aware Adaptive Optimization strategy is incorporated during the inference phase. By dynamically tracking the local spatial folding status, it adaptively adjusts spatial regularization to effectively suppress topological distortions while maximizing voxel-level accuracy. Main results. Extensive experiments on mono-modal, multi-modal, and pathological brain MRI datasets demonstrate that our method can handle large anatomical deformations without relying on external training datasets. It achieves highly competitive registration performance compared to mainstream population-based and implicit neural representation methods. Crucially, it balances this alignment precision with effective numerical topology preservation. Significance. This framework challenges the traditional population-based learning paradigm, offering a highly flexible, robust, and promising solution for practical neuroimage analysis, particularly in clinical scenarios characterized by extreme data scarcity and complex cross-modality variations.

title: Bidirectional multi-scale implicit neural representation network for topology-aware lung 4D-CT registration.
abstract: Objective. Precise lung 4D-CT registration is extremely challenging due to large respiratory excursions. To capture such large-magnitude motion, existing deep learning methods typically adopt a unidirectional coarse-to-fine cascade strategy, which is vulnerable to error propagation because uncorrected coarse-level misalignments degrade subsequent finer-scale stages and often lead to spatially inconsistent deformations. While implicit neural representations (INRs) support continuous coordinate-based deformation modeling, traditional instance-specific INRs lack clinical efficiency and struggle to converge on global large deformations because of the absence of multi-scale semantic guidance. This study aims to bridge these gaps by developing a bidirectional multi-scale INR network that jointly handles large deformation modeling and localized structural fidelity. Approach. We propose a bidirectional multi-scale INR network. First, a generalized conditional INR framework is introduced to enable continuous deformation modeling without the need for retraining. Crucially, a bidirectional feature feedback mechanism built upon Swin Transformer injects high-level semantic priors into low-resolution streams, correcting coarse-level biases through top-down interaction. Furthermore, an anatomy-aware structural constraint is incorporated to promote anatomical consistency and local boundary alignment. Main results. Under the within-subject phase-held-out DIR-Lab protocol, the proposed method achieved a mean TRE of 1.28 mm and a folding rate of 0.0090%. A leave-one-case-out evaluation assessed subject-independent generalization, yielding a mean TRE of 1.53 mm and a folding rate of 0.0195%. On the independent POPI dataset, the method achieved a mean TRE of 1.84 mm and a folding rate of 0.0806%, demonstrating competitive cross-center performance. Inference took 0.33 s per case. Significance. The proposed framework effectively combines continuous coordinate modeling with deep learning efficiency, overcoming error propagation inherent in discrete coarse-to-fine strategies and preserving both global deformation consistency and local anatomical precision. Its sub-second inference and performance under leave-one-case-out and independent external testing support its potential for efficient image-guided radiation therapy workflows.

title: EFM-GAN: enhanced feature modeling for multimodal MRI synthesis under missing-modality settings.
abstract: Objective . Multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) synthesis has been widely investigated for recovering unavailable imaging modalities under incomplete acquisition scenarios. However, existing approaches often rely on implicit feature fusion strategies, where modality-specific appearance information and cross-modal anatomical representations are entangled in a shared latent space. Such entanglement may lead to unstable feature interaction and limit the preservation of modality-invariant structural information. Moreover, although multimodal MRI sequences are generally spatially registered, modality-specific acquisition mechanisms introduce heterogeneous feature distributions, leading to feature-level semantic inconsistency during cross-modal representation learning. Lesion-related details are also frequently underrepresented, particularly in anatomically complex regions that are difficult to reconstruct. Approach . To address these limitations, an enhanced feature modeling generative adversarial network (EFM-GAN) is proposed with an explicit parallel feature modeling framework. In EFM-GAN, parallel feature branches explicitly model modality-specific appearance and cross-modal shared representations. A bidirectional progressive alignment module is further introduced to progressively reduce feature-level semantic discrepancies between modality-specific representations before feature fusion, while preserving modality-dependent appearance information. Furthermore, a reconstruction difficulty-aware loss is designed to adaptively reweight reconstruction constraints, assigning greater emphasis to regions that are harder to reconstruct. Main results . Extensive experiments on the BRaTS2020 and BRaTS2021 datasets demonstrate that EFM-GAN achieves higher peak signal-to-noise ratio and structural similarity index than the evaluated baseline methods across multiple target modalities, with improved structural consistency and synthesis fidelity. Significance . The results demonstrate the effectiveness of explicitly modeling modality-specific and shared representations, progressively aligning heterogeneous features, and emphasizing reconstruction-difficult regions for missing-modality MRI synthesis.

title: Volumetric chest CT report generation via state-space visual prompting and clinical-fact alignment.
abstract: Objective. To address the memory bottlenecks of three-dimensional (3D) sequence modeling and the factual hallucinations associated with cross-entropy optimization in automated 3D chest computed tomography (CT) report generation. Approach. We propose an end-to-end framework that couples perception refinement with clinical-fact alignment. First, a hybrid perception module integrates spatial visual encoding with a bidirectional state-space model to capture global anatomical topology at linear computational complexity. Second, a lesion-aware visual prompting module extracts key pathological signals through cross-view synergy and adaptive residual gating. Finally, the text decoder is fine-tuned with the group relative policy optimization algorithm under an asymmetric composite reward, reducing its reliance on normal templates. Main results. Experiments on the CTRG-Chest-548K dataset show that the proposed method achieves competitive natural language generation performance and, more importantly, a substantial improvement in clinical accuracy. The RadGraph1 score increases from 41.89 to 44.63 relative to the strongest baseline, indicating reduced factual hallucination. Significance. Combined with a 71% reduction in peak inference memory, these results indicate that the framework is a practical step toward deployable and clinically reliable automated CT interpretation.

title: 3D ultrasound shear wave elastography quantifies myocardial stiffness and anisotropy in the human heart.
abstract: Myocardial stiffness (MS) is a key property of diastolic cardiac function which is altered in various cardiomyopathies. Its quantitative evaluation remains challenging due to the myocardium's complex anisotropic fibers architecture and dynamic contraction. We developed a novel 3D shear wave elastography (3D-SWE) system suitable for clinical translation based on 3D ultrafast volumetric imaging for the quantitative assessment of MS in the human heart. Validation was performed on calibrated phantoms and ex vivo in porcine hearts compared to standard 2D-SWE. In vivo feasibility was demonstrated on healthy volunteers and patients with transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (CA). We demonstrated that 3D shear wave propagation can be observed in vivo and that 3D-SWE provides quantitative assessment of myocardium anisotropy through shear wave velocities along and across fibers and fractional anisotropy. In addition, MS was significantly elevated in CA patients compared to normal myocardium, whereas the fractional anisotropy was decreased. The feasibility of volumetric MS mapping on the human heart was demonstrated showing the potential of 3D-SWE as a clinically oriented tool for early diagnosis of cardiomyopathies such as CA.

title: 3D non-rigid motion correction using Doppler-regularized optical flow for coronary ultrasound localization microscopy in beating heart.
abstract: Objectives . Coronary microvascular disease, involving vessels smaller than 300 µ m, contributes significantly to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. However, direct visualization of coronary microcirculation remains challenging because current clinical imaging modalities lack the spatial and temporal resolution required to resolve the microvascular network. Ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) enables imaging beyond the diffraction limit and can reveal coronary microvascular structures but is altered by large motion. This work addresses 3D non-rigid motion in coronary ULM to enable more accurate reconstruction and visualization of the coronary microvascular network. Approach . Here we developed a 3D non-rigid motion correction framework based on optical flow with Doppler velocity regularization to compensate for cardiac motion in 3D ULM of beating rat hearts. Main results . The method was validated in perfused ex vivo beating rat hearts imaged with ultrafast 3D ultrasound. Motion correction enhanced microbubbles tracking density and vessels delineation, enabling visualization of microvessels below 100 µ m and velocity measurements with spatial resolution of at least 40 µ m. Significance . This framework advances volumetric assessment of coronary microcirculation, facilitating longer acquisition windows and may support future cardiovascular research and clinical applications by overcoming motion-induced limitations in 3D coronary ULM.

title: Motion-guided semi-supervised learning with dynamic kernels for cardiac cine segmentation.
abstract: Objective. Accurate segmentation of full cardiac cine magnetic resonance sequences is crucial for clinical diagnosis. Although deep learning models have become the standard for this task, they typically require exhaustive frame-by-frame supervision, making manual data annotation prohibitively time-consuming. Approach. To address this, we propose an integrated motion-guided semi-supervised spatiotemporal framework that propagates sparse supervision from the label of the end-diastolic (ED) frame to the entire sequence. Our framework jointly optimizes motion estimation and segmentation. First, a motion decoder estimates dense displacement fields to warp the ED label, generating high-fidelity pseudo-labels for unannotated frames. Concurrently, the segmentation network employs a temporal kernel segmentation module with dynamic convolutions to adaptively capture rapid cardiac deformations, alongside a multi-scale spatial propagator to recover fine anatomical boundaries. The motion-derived pseudo-labels directly supervise the segmentation network, ensuring temporal coherence. Main results. Extensive experiments on a multi-center cohort from three clinical centers demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms the compared methods, achieving superior segmentation accuracy and robust generalization capabilities. Significance. The proposed framework effectively mitigates the burden of manual data annotation while providing temporally coherent full-cycle cardiac analysis, holding significant potential for efficient and reliable clinical assessment of cardiovascular diseases.

title: Segmentation-perturbation propagation in pretrained foundation-model embeddings versus IBSI-aligned radiomics for radiologist-assessed lung-nodule malignancy classification on the LIDC-IDRI cohort.
abstract: Objective Pretrained foundation-model (FM) embeddings are proposed as robust alternatives to handcrafted radiomic features, yet whether they better withstand segmentation-mask variability, the perturbation that radiomics intraclass-correlation (ICC) filtering exists to address, has not been tested head-to-head. We quantified how segmentation-mask perturbation propagates into feature reproducibility and downstream malignancy discrimination for FM embeddings and Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI)-compliant radiomics measured on a common cohort. Approach. Two 2D FM encoders (BiomedCLIP; RadImageNet ResNet50) were compared against IBSI-compliant radiomics (3D, 107 features; 2D, 102 features) on the full eligible Lung Image Database Consortium and Image Database Resource Initiative (LIDC-IDRI) cohort: 556 lung nodules (300 malignant, 256 benign from radiologist consensus ratings, not pathology) from 399 patients. Up to thirteen perturbed masks per nodule (up to four reader masks, eight synthetic, one Dice-calibrated) were generated, and ICC(2,1) was computed across the ten perturbation conditions available for every nodule. Malignancy classification used L2-regularized logistic regression with patient-grouped five-fold cross-validation and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on every area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Main results. Radiomics outperformed both foundation models on discrimination (AUC 0.940 and 0.930 for radiomics-2D/3D versus 0.833 BiomedCLIP and 0.798 RadImageNet; all radiomics-versus-FM differences significant by DeLong test, p≤10^(-7)). On perturbation stability the foundation models diverged: BiomedCLIP was statistically indistinguishable from radiomics (93.8% versus 90.2-92.5% stable features) and the most stable paradigm, whereas RadImageNet was significantly less stable (75.0%). A pre-specified diameter-stratified analysis showed the radiomics advantage narrows, and partly reverses, within size-matched strata; decision-curve analysis favoured radiomics. Significance. Two-dimensional foundation-model embeddings offered no discrimination advantage over IBSI radiomics under segmentation perturbation, and greater stability did not translate into greater accuracy. Perturbation stability is therefore decoupled from task-informativeness, and comparative benchmarks should report patient-grouped, size-stratified, calibration-aware metrics, not aggregate accuracy alone.&#xD.

title: Quantifying multi-lesion detection and localization in whole-body FDG PET/CT with a multimodal foundation model.
abstract: Objective . To develop a three-dimensional AI framework for detecting and localizing multiple lesions in whole-body FDG PET/CT, and to evaluate whether a pretrained PET/CT multimodal foundation model can improve lesion detection performance compared with conventional training from scratch. Approach . The AutoPET cohort comprised 1014 studies divided into 700 training, 114 validation, and 200 subject-independent test studies. Lesion masks were converted into three-dimensional bounding boxes. We developed a one-stage 3D lesion detector using a PlainConvUNet backbone to extract multi-scale encoder-decoder features for lesion classification and box regression. To leverage foundation-model representations, the PlainConvUNet backbone was initialized with weights from our previously developed multi-center PET/CT multimodal foundation model, pretrained using masked autoencoding, and subsequently fine-tuned for lesion detection. Four configurations were compared: PET+CT trained from scratch, PET only, CT only, and PET+CT initialized from the pretrained PET/CT foundation model. Detection performance was evaluated using free-response receiver operating characteristic (FROC) and alternative FROC (AFROC) analyses, sensitivity at fixed false-positive (FP) rates, qualitative analysis, and lesion-size-stratified operating curves. Main results . Multimodal PET+CT consistently outperformed either modality alone across task-based detection metrics, demonstrating the complementary contributions of metabolic and anatomical information. Importantly, initialization from the pretrained PET/CT multimodal foundation model further enhanced lesion detection performance compared with training the same PET+CT detector from scratch, increasing absolute FROC sensitivity by 0.034-0.041 across the evaluated 1-4 FP-per-scan operating range and improving AFROC AUC by 0.028. Detection performance increased with lesion size, with small lesions remaining the most challenging. The separation between the pretrained and randomly initialized PET+CT configurations was more evident in the smaller-lesion strata, whereas their operating curves increasingly overlapped for larger lesions. Significance . This study provides a detection-centered, task-based characterization of multi-lesion analysis in whole-body PET/CT. Multimodal PET+CT improves lesion detection compared with either modality alone, lesion size is a major determinant of detection performance, and initialization from a pretrained PET/CT multimodal foundation model provides an additional performance improvement without modifying the downstream detector architecture.

title: Experimental validation of skull acoustic modelling strategies for transcranial focused ultrasound simulation: a cross-comparison study.
abstract: Objective. Accurate acoustic modelling of the skull is important for simulation-guided transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) applications. However, existing skull parameterization strategies vary widely in complexity and reported accuracy. This study systematically evaluates commonly used modelling approaches to determine their predictive performance across multiple frequencies and skull types. Approach. Five skull modelling strategies were assessed: two voxel-wise linear mapping models, one with fixed attenuation coefficient and one with Hounsfield unit-dependent attenuation coefficients; two three-layer models with fixed and skull-density ratio dependent attenuation coefficient; and one single-layer fixed-parameter model. Nineteen regions of interest from five historical and two Thiel-embalmed human skulls were examined at 220 kHz, 680 kHz and 1000 kHz, bowl-surface source fields were reconstructed using holography, and intracranial pressure distributions were captured with a needle hydrophone. Measurements were compared with k -Wave simulations. Results. Average simulated peak pressure errors ( ɛ p ) ranged from 20%-31% across frequencies, whereas intensity errors ( ɛ I ) reached 41% to 81%. Errors in -6 dB focal volume ranged from 18%-65%, and focal position discrepancies were typically several millimetres. Simulation generally predicted smaller insertion losses than measured, indicating a tendency to underestimate skull-related attenuation and overestimate transmitted intracranial exposure. Among the five modelling strategies, the model with the lowest observed error varied with frequency and outcome. Paired specimen-level comparisons did not establish a consistent accuracy advantage for any strategy. Significance. These results indicate that current skull modelling strategies may reproduce the gross intracranial beam pattern while still misestimating the delivered acoustic exposure, focal coverage and localization. Such errors are directly relevant to tFUS dose selection, target coverage and safety-margin interpretation, underscoring the need for refined parameterization methods for reliable tFUS treatment planning.

title: Artificial intelligence for cerebrovascular digital subtraction angiography: methods, evidence, and challenges.
abstract: Cerebrovascular diseases remain a major cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) provides high-spatiotemporal-resolution visualization of cerebrovascular anatomy and contrast-agent dynamics and plays an important role in diagnosis, interventional treatment planning, and treatment assessment. Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been applied to cerebrovascular DSA, yet the available evidence is distributed across diverse imaging settings, technical tasks, datasets, and validation strategies. This structured topical review provides a DSA-centered overview of AI-assisted cerebrovascular image analysis across 2D DSA, three-dimensional rotational angiography, and four-dimensional DSA. Literature from Web of Science Core Collection and major engineering databases was screened at title, abstract, and full-text levels using predefined eligibility criteria. The literature is organized around six interconnected tasks: image preprocessing, vessel and lesion segmentation, image registration, reconstruction and generation, disease diagnosis and detection, and hemodynamic analysis. Representative conventional and learning-based methods are reviewed together with their datasets, evaluation metrics, validation designs, and available data or code resources, with particular attention to the strength and limitations of the supporting evidence. Recent studies demonstrate increasing use of spatiotemporal modeling, deep learning, and image-generation techniques, but clinical translation remains constrained by small or single-center datasets, heterogeneous acquisition protocols and evaluation practices, limited external and prospective validation, model interpretability, and deployment requirements. Future work should emphasize acquisition-aware and physics-informed modeling, multicenter and privacy-preserving collaboration, clinically meaningful validation, and closer integration with neurointerventional workflows. By linking methodological developments with their supporting evidence and translational challenges, this review aims to support the development of more robust and clinically applicable AI methods for cerebrovascular DSA.

title: SPARC: sectorized partial-angle reconstruction based motion correction method for multi-phase CCTA.
abstract: Objective. Multi-phase coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) provides a clear visualization of coronary arteries, offering comprehensive and reliable imaging support for the clinical diagnosis of coronary artery disease. However, traditional motion correction reconstruction algorithms lack reconstruction robustness despite their interpretability, while deep learning reconstruction methods achieve high imaging quality at the expense of interpretability and anatomical reliability in clinical CCTA practice. This study aims to simultaneously achieve interpretable and robust multi-phase coronary reconstruction. Approach. We propose a motion trajectory estimation and motion correction framework termed sectorized partial-angle reconstruction-based motion correction (SPARC) for CCTA. The proposed framework integrates sectorized partial-angle reconstructions, a spatio-temporal cascaded network for coronary centerline extraction, and a phase-accumulated fuzzy C-means clustering algorithm for motion trajectory estimation. These components work together to minimize motion estimation errors and enhance the quality of motion-corrected reconstruction. Main results . Experimental results from both simulations and clinical studies demonstrate that SPARC achieves superior reconstruction performance compared with existing methods. SPARC effectively reduces coronary motion artifacts and restores clear vessel structures while preserving reconstruction fidelity, achieving the best scores on all metrics. Significance. By preserving both interpretability and anatomical reliability while effectively reducing motion artifacts, SPARC provides a clinically deployable solution for motion-corrected multi-phase CCTA, supporting more reliable imaging for coronary artery disease diagnosis.

title: Sampling-free Monte Carlo dropout approximation for single-pass uncertainty quantification in deep learning-based PET reconstructions.
abstract: Objective . Medical image reconstructions using deep learning (DL) can rapidly generate high-quality images from degraded measurements, but their clinical adoption remains challenging, largely due to the lack of fast and reliable methods to quantify aleatoric (data-driven) and epistemic (model-driven) uncertainties on a per-prediction basis. We aim to develop a computationally efficient approach for estimating both uncertainties at the voxel level in DL-based image reconstruction within a single inference run. Approach . We present a moment propagation-based framework that analytically approximates the conventional, multi-realization Monte Carlo (MC) dropout by propagating feature-map means and marginal variances through network layers, followed by a pre-calibrated correction table to compensate for covariance effects omitted in the approximation. This enables joint estimation of reconstruction, aleatoric uncertainty and epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass. The proposed framework was implemented on top of FastPET-a network model synthesizing PET reconstructions from time-of-flight histo-images-and evaluated in a patient pilot study of 26 total-body PET/CT acquisitions (16F-FDG and 10F-PSMA cases). Main results . Proposed method achieved relatively strong agreement with the 50-pass MC approach, with absolute differences0.5% for reconstruction,4.2% for aleatoric uncertainty and9.8% for epistemic uncertainty, along with narrow spreads across patients and tracer types, while reducing computation time by40-fold. In a complementary proof-of-concept low-count experiment, regional tracer uptake confidence intervals (CIs, derived from propagated uncertainties) widened with increased noise level, and reference uptakes consistently fell within and close to CI boundaries, indicating the proposed method could provide roughly calibrated uncertainty magnitudes reflecting quantitative prediction errors. Significance . The proposed approach provides a sampling-free and relatively accurate approximation to the multi-pass MC-based uncertainty estimation in the histo-image-based DL PET reconstruction framework. Per-prediction uncertainty quantification enables direct assessment of AI confidence and potentially supports more reliable and informed decision-making.

title: Closed-form, engine-portable uncertainty prediction of deformable image registration for dose accumulation in adaptive radiotherapy.
abstract: Objective. Voxel-level uncertainty estimates of the deformation vector field (DVF) produced by commercial deformable image registration (DIR) engines are flagged as an open issue by AAPM TG-132 but seldom available, preventing principled propagation into accumulated dose-volume histograms (DVHs). We propose and validate an engine-portable per-voxelpredictor for the DVF () of a deterministic DIR, calibrated by one scalaragainst landmark target registration error (TRE), with no access to the engine's internals. Approach. The framework combines (i) an anisotropic Gaussian correlation kernel, longer along the cranio-caudal axis, generalising the isotropic kernel of Smolders et al (2023); and (ii) a heuristic-residual(default), wherecombines a self-similarity descriptor residual with an image-gradient suppression factor andis, both normalised to;is closed-form, computed from the image pair and the DVF without optimisation or training. For each combination of dataset and DIR engine (a cell),is calibrated against TRE via grid search minimising the Landmark Expected Calibration Error (LECE). Main results. Across 4 publicly annotated computed tomography datasets (Lung-, Abdominal- and Liver-DIR-QA and DIR-LAB Castillo; 44 778 landmarks) and 4 DIR engines (ANTs SyNRA, ConvexAdam, uniGradICON, Elastix), withfitted on other patients (5-fold cross-validation), the calibratedachieves, in the per-direction convention of Smolders et al LECE within or below their 0.41-1.34 mm range in all 16 cells (cases with final root-mean-square TREmm retained). A constantcalibrated likewise also meets this range, but the variation ofraises the held-out log-likelihood in 13 cells;ranks landmarks by error only weakly (Spearmanto). Significance. A one-scalar, post-hoc calibration yields voxel-level DVF uncertainty for any deterministic DIR that exports its DVF, partly addressing the AAPM TG-132 gap; propagation into accumulated DVH bands is illustrated on one lung stereotactic body radiotherapy case.

title: Magnetic resonance thermometry-based estimation of equivalent radiation dose and tumour control probability in combined radiotherapy and hyperthermia: a proof-of-concept and uncertainty study.
abstract: Objective To estimate the equivalent radiation dose in 2 Gy fractions (EQD2Gy) and tumour control probability (TCP) from probe based and magnetic resonance (MR) temperature measurements. In addition, we evaluate how uncertainties in MR thermometry affect these metrics in combined radiotherapy and hyperthermia for locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC). Approach: Temperature data were collected from three patients with LACC treated with radiotherapy and MR guided deep hyperthermia (MRgHT). Intraluminal vaginal probes provided temperature measurements at surrogate locations, while MR thermometry enabled voxel-wise temperature mapping within the target volume. These data were used to estimate EQD2Gy and TCP for combined radiotherapy and hyperthermia treatments. To assess the robustness of MR-based estimates, systematic and random temperature errors were introduced into MR thermometry data using Gaussian error models to simulate artefacts. The resulting impact on temperature distributions, EQD2Gy and TCP was evaluated using standard deviation analysis and dose volume histograms. Main results: Probe-based temperatures ranged from 39.1-39.7 °C, resulting in EQD2Gy and TCP enhancements of 2.4-4.3 Gy and 20-57 %, respectively. MR-based temperatures were higher (39.4-40.3 °C), yielding EQD2Gy (3.4-7.1 Gy) and TCP (22-68 %). Systematic temperature errors produced changes of up to 2 Gy in EQD2Gy and 5 % in TCP. In contrast, random errors - more representative of typical MR thermometry artefacts - led to minimal deviations, with changes of approximately 0.2 Gy in EQD2Gy. Within clinically relevant temperature ranges, overall uncertainties remained limited to 0.7 Gy for EQD2Gy and 1 % for TCP. Significance: MR thermometry enables voxel-based estimation of biological treatment enhancement in combined radiotherapy and hyperthermia. Despite inherent temperature uncertainties, MR-based EQD2Gy and TCP estimates remain robust within clinical accuracy limits, supporting their use for treatment evaluation and future hyperthermia-informed treatment planning.

title: Capturing reader-specific annotation biases in ordinal classification: a controlled simulation study.
abstract: Objective. Inter-reader variability remains a major challenge in medical image classification, particularly for tasks involving ordinal labels, due to subjective interpretation and institutional biases. While deep learning is widely used to automate and standardize such classification tasks, including breast density assessment, handling reader-dependent annotation behavior remains an open problem. This study introduces a controlled setting to assess the extent to which such variability can be captured by a reader-adaptive model. Approach. This work builds on ReaderAdaptNet, a recently proposed reader-adaptive framework that models individual annotation styles through jointly learned reader-specific embeddings. Through a simulation study, it aims to deepen the understanding of this framework and to address the evaluation limitations imposed by small expert-annotated datasets, for which the underlying bias mechanisms are neither known nor controllable. Synthetic reader profiles are generated to reproduce realistic annotation behaviors, enabling a controlled analysis of the model's ability to adapt to diverse annotation biases. The effects of the embedding dimension and of the fusion strategy of image-reader features on classification accuracy are assessed. The structure of the embedding space is also analyzed. Main results. Results show that reader embeddings effectively capture identifiable, systematic biases, with moderate embedding dimensionality being sufficient. Systematic threshold shifts are recovered, whereas stochastic variability is not learnable. Conditioning image-reader fusion through feature-wise linear modulation or cross-attention mechanisms enables the correction of view-related discrepancies. The learned embedding space further reveals meaningful clustering of annotation profiles, reflecting similarity in reader behavior. Significance. Overall, the proposed synthetic framework identifies which aspects of inter-reader variability are learnable by ReaderAdaptNet and provides a controlled proxy for anticipating model behavior in clinical settings.

title: Enhanced diffusion model with 3D structural and segmentation priors for lung cancer radiotherapy dose prediction.
abstract: Objective Diffusion models show strong potential for high-fidelity radiotherapy dose prediction, but their performance depends heavily on the conditioning mechanism. This study introduces a novel conditioning strategy that improves volumetric consistency in slice-wise dose generation while reducing reliance on manually annotated organ-at-risk (OAR) masks. Approach We propose a diffusion-based dose prediction framework conditioned on features from the full 3D computed tomography (CT) volume and a pre-trained medical image segmentation model. A 3D feature extractor encodes global anatomical information from the entire CT volume to preserve spatial coherence across 2D dose predictions. Rather than relying on manual OAR masks, the model uses anatomical representations from the pre-trained segmentation network, integrated via cross-attention to enable anatomy-aware dose prediction. Main results The framework, Diff-Seg3D, was evaluated on three lung cancer radiotherapy datasets representing Volumetric Modulated Arc Therapy (VMAT), Fixed Gantry Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy (FGIMRT), and 3D Conformal Radiation Therapy (3DCRT) planning techniques. It achieved the numerically lowest mean absolute error (MAE) on all three datasets, with values of 3.16, 4.38, and 4.02 Gy, respectively, and the best dose-volume histogram (DVH) scores (2.64 and 3.82) on VMAT and FGIMRT, while remaining competitive on 3DCRT. Pre-trained 3D anatomical and segmentation encoders improved the baseline diffusion model, with segmentation features improving performance without requiring explicit OAR contours at inference. Significance This conditioning strategy improves volumetric consistency and anatomical awareness in diffusion-based dose prediction. The framework can serve as a tool for generating treatment-specific, anatomy-conditioned dose priors to guide radiotherapy planning.

title: NOZOMI: a GPU-accelerated Monte-Carlo numerical approach for microstructure diffusion imaging.
abstract: Objective To develop an open-source computational framework for generating realistic white matter substrates and performing Monte-Carlo diffusion MRI simulations that use periodic boundary conditions to avoid artificial restrictions at substrate boundaries. Approach: A) A novel substrate generation algorithm was developed that ensures microstructure continuity across boundaries by adding reciprocal and replicated axons for boundary-crossing axons during substrate generation. B) A dedicated GPU-accelerated Monte-Carlo diffusion simulation engine was included, with multi-threaded CUDA implementation and simulation domain segmentation for computational efficiency. C) Validation and calibration experiments were done to verify geometric continuity across periodic boundaries, confirm simulation accuracy and precision against analytical solutions across diffusion times, compare against established simulators (Camino, Disimpy, MC/DC) under finite-pulse protocols, and guide simulation configuration. D) Diffusion time dependent axial and radial diffusivities across substrates with varying mean axon diameters and orientation dispersions were evaluated to demonstrate the utility of the framework. Main results: The framework successfully constructed complex biomimetic white matter substrates achieving high packing densities with controlled diameter distributions, orientation dispersions, beading morphology, and myelination. Monte-Carlo simulations reveal that, in both intra- and extra-axonal spaces, axon diameter primarily influences time-dependent radial diffusion, while fiber orientation dispersion primarily impacts axial diffusion. Significance: The developed framework is the first 3D white matter simulation framework to implement periodic boundary conditions for Monte-Carlo simulations without geometric discontinuity, providing approximately four times faster substrate generation than comparable tools, while facilitating controlled investigations of compartment-specific diffusion time dependence of microstructure-diffusion relationships.

title: Test-retest repeatability of MBSS-T1: a model-based, subject-specific self-supervised motion correction method for robust cardiac T1 mapping.
abstract: Objective Reliable myocardial T1 mapping is essential for quantitative cardiac tissue characterization but remains sensitive to respiratory motion, particularly during free-breathing acquisitions. This study evaluated the test-retest repeatability of MBSS-T1, a subject-specific, model-based, self-supervised deep-learning method for motion-robust myocardial T1 mapping. Approach. Seventeen healthy male volunteers aged 20-36 years underwent 3 T cardiac MRI using a 5(3)3 MOLLI acquisition under breath-hold (BH) and free-breathing (FB) conditions. Same-day repeat scans were acquired after a 20 min interval that included removal from and repositioning in the scanner. T1 maps were reconstructed using (1) MBSS-T1, (2) the contrast-agnostic deep-learning registration method SynthMorph, (3) scanner-inline motion correction, and (4) no motion correction. Repeatability was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), relative Bland-Altman analysis, within-subject coefficients of variation (CVw), relative 95% repeatability coefficients (RC95), and variance-based bootstrap inference with Holm correction. Main results. All four methods included 17 complete participant-level test-retest pairs under each breathing condition. Under BH conditions, the global ICC point estimates were 0.77, 0.64, 0.65, and 0.60 for MBSS-T1, SynthMorph, scanner-inline correction, and no correction, respectively. Under FB conditions, the corresponding values were 0.41, 0.32, 0.27, and 0.16. MBSS-T1 also had the lowest descriptive CVw under both conditions. However, none of the paired comparisons of absolute test-retest differences was significant after Holm correction (all adjusted p ≥ 0.623). The smallest Holm-adjusted variance-ratio result was obtained for MBSS-T1 versus no correction under FB conditions (variance ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.30-0.68; adjusted p = 0.058), which did not meet the prespecified significance threshold. Significance. MBSS-T1 yielded favourable descriptive repeatability estimates, particularly under FB conditions, but no pairwise comparison remained statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. These results characterize same-day, same-scanner measurement precision rather than absolute T1 accuracy and require confirmation in larger and more clinically diverse cohorts.

title: In silico feasibility and robustness evaluation of a single-spot proton Bragg peak FLASH platform for small-animal irradiation using a generalized 3D-printed bolus.
abstract: Objective FLASH radiotherapy has shown potential to reduce normal tissue toxicity while maintaining tumour control, motivating the development of clinical delivery strategies. However, most preclinical proton FLASH studies rely on transmission beams or spread out Bragg peaks, which do not reflect conformal clinical dose distributions. This work aims to develop and evaluate an irradiation setup for ultra-high dose-rate Bragg peak proton delivery to orthotopic mammary tumours in mice, employable in image-guided research rooms powered by clinical cyclotrons. Approach We built a simulation framework (Python+TOPAS) to assess a single spot, ablative configuration comprising a copper degrader, collimator, and generalised (3D-printed) bolus. Performance was investigated on a Phantom Mice Cohort (N=6) using personalised boluses and a Real Mice Cohort (N=10; µCT/PET) using a cohort-derived generalised bolus. Planning goals were D99%,GTV=19.0Gy and HIGTV≤1.30. Physical dose-rate feasibility was evaluated against a nominal 40Gy/s DRmin,skin threshold under an assumed 500nA beam current cap; this metric does not establish a biological FLASH effect. Robustness evaluation included 0.35 and 0.5mm setup errors and ±3% range uncertainties. Main results Simulated plans met target and heterogeneity goals across cohorts, with the 40Gy/s DRmin,skin criterion met under the assumed beam current conditions (Dmean,skin≈18.5-19.3Gy). The modelled dose-rate criterion was met below the 500nA beam current limit in both cohorts. Under the evaluated 0.35mm setup and ±3% range uncertainties, reduction in D99%,GTV remained within 3% for 9/10 real mouse cases. The generalised bolus achieved the simulated dosimetric performance across ten anatomically distinct mice; applicability to independent cohorts remains unestablished. Significance This in silico evaluation supports the simulated dosimetric and physical dose-rate feasibility of conformal Bragg peak proton delivery in small animals using a generalised bolus. The presented framework enables further development in image-guided proton research facilities, forming a strong basis for experimental validation and commissioning toward in situ small animal studies.&#xD.

title: Differential priors guided adaptive multi-scale edge-guided attention for medical image synthesis with stable diffusion.
abstract: Abstract Objective. Diffusion models pretrained on natural images provide a useful basis for medical image synthesis, but preserving lesion structure remains challenging when annotated data are limited. We aim to improve the quality and segmentation utility of mask-conditioned synthetic images. Approach. We propose a structure-aware fine-tuning framework based on Stable Diffusion and ControlNet. Adaptive Multi-scale Edge-Guided Attention (AMEGA) integrates first-order Sobel and second-order Laplacian responses with multi-scale features. A complementary training objective combines foreground and background supervision with adaptive boundary regularization to encourage structural consistency during generation. Main results. Experiments on BMRI, ISIC2016, and Kvasir-SEG evaluate image quality and downstream segmentation. Compared with mask-conditioned SD+ControlNet, the framework reduces dataset-averaged FID by 18.2% and improves mean downstream Dice from 0 . 711 to 0 .736. Significance. Integrating differential features and boundary-aware supervision improves medical image synthesis and supports synthetic-data augmentation under limited annotations.
